In this exercise: 1. Find A.M. between. 2. If 3 and 8 are two A.Ms. between a and b, find a and b. 3. Insert three A.Ms. between 4 and 17. 4. Insert four A.Ms. between √(3) and 12/√(3). 5. Find six A.Ms. between -15 and 15. 6. Find n so that (x^{n+4} + y^{n+4})/(x^{n+3} + y^{n+3}) may be the A.M. between x and y. 7. Find the values of x if |1 0; 0 4| is the A.M. between |x 1; 1 x+2| and |1 0; 0 4|. (Determinants written row-wise.).

Worked Example: 1. Find A.M. between. (i) 9 and 16; (ii) 6 + 2 √(7) and 4 - 2 √(7); (iii) 3x + 2y and 5x - 6y; (iv) 3 + 4 √(3) i and 9 - 4 √(3) i; (v) 3x^2 - 5x + 6 and -x^2 + 7x - 4; (vi) 3x - 5 and 5x + 3.

Formula used: A.M. = (a + b) / 2; n means between a and b: d = (b - a) / (n + 1).

Step 1: The arithmetic mean (A.M.) between a and b is (a + b)/2.

Step 2: (i) (9 + 16)/2 = 25/2.

Step 3: (ii) (6 + 2 √(7) + 4 - 2 √(7))/2 = 10/2 = 5.

Step 4: (iii) (3x + 2y + 5x - 6y)/2 = (8x - 4y)/2 = 4x - 2y.

Step 5: (iv) (3 + 4 √(3) i + 9 - 4 √(3) i)/2 = 12/2 = 6.

Step 6: (v) (3x^2 - 5x + 6 - x^2 + 7x - 4)/2 = (2x^2 + 2x + 2)/2 = x^2 + x + 1.

Step 7: (vi) (3x - 5 + 5x + 3)/2 = (8x - 2)/2 = 4x - 1.

Answer: (i) 25/2; (ii) 5; (iii) 4x - 2y; (iv) 6; (v) x^2 + x + 1; (vi) 4x - 1

Worked Example: 3. Insert three A.Ms. between 4 and 17.

Formula used: A.M. = (a + b) / 2; n means between a and b: d = (b - a) / (n + 1).

Step 1: Inserting three means gives 5 terms in A.P.: first term 4, fifth term 17.

Step 2: Let the common difference be d: 4 + 4d = 17, so 4d = 13, d = 13/4.

Step 3: The three means are: 4 + 13/4 = 29/4; 4 + 2(13/4) = 4 + 13/2 = 21/2; 4 + 3(13/4) = 55/4.

Answer: 29/4, 21/2, 55/4

Worked Example: 4. Insert four A.Ms. between √(3) and 12/√(3).

Formula used: A.M. = (a + b) / 2; n means between a and b: d = (b - a) / (n + 1).

Step 1: Note 12/√(3) = 4 √(3). Inserting four means gives 6 terms in A.P.: first term √(3), sixth term 4 √(3).

Step 2: Let the common difference be d: √(3) + 5d = 4 √(3), so 5d = 3 √(3), d = (3 √(3))/5.

Step 3: The four means are: √(3) + (3 √(3))/5 = (8 √(3))/5; (11 √(3))/5; (14 √(3))/5; (17 √(3))/5.

Answer: (8 √(3))/5, (11 √(3))/5, (14 √(3))/5, (17 √(3))/5

Worked Example: 5. Find six A.Ms. between -15 and 15.

Formula used: A.M. = (a + b) / 2; n means between a and b: d = (b - a) / (n + 1).

Step 1: Inserting six means gives 8 terms in A.P.: first term -15, eighth term 15.

Step 2: Let the common difference be d: -15 + 7d = 15, so 7d = 30, d = 30/7.

Step 3: The six means are: -15 + 30/7 = -75/7; -45/7; -15/7; 15/7; 45/7; 75/7.

Answer: -75/7, -45/7, -15/7, 15/7, 45/7, 75/7

Worked Example: 7. Find the values of x if |1 0; 0 4| is the A.M. between |x 1; 1 x+2| and |1 0; 0 4|. (Determinants written row-wise.)

Formula used: A.M. = (a + b) / 2; n means between a and b: d = (b - a) / (n + 1).

Step 1: Evaluate the determinants: |1 0; 0 4| = 4; |x 1; 1 x+2| = x(x + 2) - 1 = x^2 + 2x - 1; the third determinant is again 4.

Step 2: The A.M. condition gives: 4 = ((x^2 + 2x - 1) + 4)/2.

Step 3: So x^2 + 2x + 3 = 8, i.e. x^2 + 2x - 5 = 0.

Step 4: By the quadratic formula: x = (-2 +- √(4 + 20))/2 = -1 +- √(6).

Answer: x = -1 + √(6) or x = -1 - √(6)

mcqs.q: Find the A.M. between 9 and 16.
Find the A.M. between 6 + 2 sqrt(7) and 4 - 2 sqrt(7).
mcqs.why: A.M. = (a + b)/2 = (6 + 2 sqrt(7) + 4 - 2 sqrt(7))/2 = 10/2 = 5, since the sqrt(7) terms cancel.

mcqs.q: Find the A.M. between 3x + 2y and 5x - 6y.
Find the A.M. between 3 + 4 sqrt(3) i and 9 - 4 sqrt(3) i.
mcqs.why: A.M. = (a + b)/2 = (3 + 4 sqrt(3) i + 9 - 4 sqrt(3) i)/2 = 12/2 = 6, since the imaginary parts cancel.

mcqs.q: Find the A.M. between 3x^2 - 5x + 6 and -x^2 + 7x - 4.
Insert three A.Ms. between 4 and 17. What is the second of the three means?
mcqs.why: Five terms in A.P.: 4 + 4d = 17 gives d = 13/4. The means are 29/4, 21/2, 55/4 in order, so the second mean is 4 + 2(13/4) = 21/2.

mcqs.q: Insert four A.Ms. between sqrt(3) and 12/sqrt(3). What is the common difference d of the A.P.?
mcqs.why: 12/sqrt(3) = 4 sqrt(3). Six terms in A.P.: sqrt(3) + 5d = 4 sqrt(3), so 5d = 3 sqrt(3) and d = (3 sqrt(3))/5.

mcqs.q: Find six A.Ms. between -15 and 15. What is the first of the six means?
mcqs.why: Eight terms in A.P.: -15 + 7d = 15 gives d = 30/7. The first mean is -15 + 30/7 = (-105 + 30)/7 = -75/7.

mcqs.q: If 3 and 8 are two A.Ms. between a and b, find a.
mcqs.why: a, 3, 8, b are in A.P. with d = 8 - 3 = 5. So a = 3 - d = 3 - 5 = -2 (and b = 8 + 5 = 13 as a check).

mcqs.q: In the determinant A.M. problem of this exercise, the values of x satisfy which equation, giving x = -1 +/- sqrt(6)?
mcqs.why: The determinants are 4, x^2 + 2x - 1 and 4. The A.M. condition 4 = ((x^2 + 2x - 1) + 4)/2 gives x^2 + 2x + 3 = 8, i.e. x^2 + 2x - 5 = 0, whose roots are -1 +/- sqrt(6).

lessons.title: Exercise 3.3 (pp.103-104) - Sum of an Arithmetic Series
lessons.notes_html:
Summing an A.P. with S_n = (n/2)[2a1 + (n - 1)d]. Watch the questions that ask for the number of terms — they give a quadratic in n, and only the sensible positive root counts.

In this exercise: 1. Sum the series. 2. Find the number of terms of the following. 3. Sum the series. 4. If S_n = n(2n + 1), then find the series. 5. Find the sum of first 600 natural numbers which are neither divisible by 2 nor by 5. 6. If S_{3n}, S_{5n}, S_{8n} are the sums of 3n, 5n and 8n terms of a_n in A.P., show that S_{8n} = 4(S_{5n} - S_{3n}). 7. The sums of n terms of two arithmetic series are in the ratio of 4n - 3 : 2n + 1. Find the ratio of their 7th terms.

Worked Example: 1. Sum the series. (i) 3 + 7 + 11 + ... + a15; (ii) 4.57 + 4.87 + 5.17 + ... + a24; (iii) 3/√(2) + 2 √(2) + 5/√(2) + ... to n terms; (iv) (y - 3b) + (y - b) + (y + b) + ... to n terms; (v) 1/(1 - √(x)) + 1/(1 - x) + 1/(1 + √(x)) + ... to n terms; (vi) 2/√(3) + √(3) + 4/√(3) + ... + a20.

Formula used: S_n = (n/2) [2a1 + (n - 1) d] = (n/2) (first term + last term).

Step 1: Use S_n = (n/2)[2a + (n - 1)d].

Step 2: (i) a = 3, d = 4, n = 15: S_15 = (15/2)[6 + 14(4)] = (15/2)(62) = 465.

Step 3: (ii) a = 4.57, d = 0.30, n = 24: S_24 = 12[9.14 + 23(0.30)] = 12(16.04) = 192.48.

Step 4: (iii) a = 3/√(2), d = 2 √(2) - 3/√(2) = 1/√(2). S_n = (n/2)[6/√(2) + (n - 1)/√(2)] = n(n + 5)/(2 √(2)) = n(n + 5) √(2)/4.

Step 5: (iv) a = y - 3b, d = 2b. S_n = (n/2)[2(y - 3b) + (n - 1)(2b)] = (n/2)[2y + 2b(n - 4)] = ny + nb(n - 4).

Step 6: (v) Let t = √(x). The terms are 1/(1 - t), 1/(1 - t^2), 1/(1 + t); consecutive differences are both -t/(1 - t^2), so d = -√(x)/(1 - x) and a = 1/(1 - √(x)). S_n = (n/2)[2/(1 - t) + (n - 1)(-t/(1 - t^2))] = n[2 + (3 - n) √(x)]/[2(1 - x)].

Step 7: (vi) a = 2/√(3), d = √(3) - 2/√(3) = 1/√(3). a_20 = 2/√(3) + 19/√(3) = 21/√(3) = 7 √(3). S_20 = 10(2/√(3) + 7 √(3)) = 10(23/√(3)) = 230/√(3) = 230 √(3)/3.

Answer: (i) 465; (ii) 192.48; (iii) n(n + 5) √(2)/4; (iv) ny + nb(n - 4); (v) n[2 + (3 - n) √(x)]/[2(1 - x)]; (vi) 230 √(3)/3

Worked Example: 3. Sum the series. (i) 3 + 5 - 7 + 10 + 12 - 14 + 17 + 19 - 21 + ... to 3n terms. (ii) 9 + 12 - 15 + 18 + 21 - 24 + 27 + 30 - 33 + ... to 3n terms.

Formula used: S_n = (n/2) [2a1 + (n - 1) d] = (n/2) (first term + last term).

Step 1: (i) Group in threes: (3, 5, -7), (10, 12, -14), ... The k-th group is (7k - 4) + (7k - 2) + (-7k) = 7k - 6. Check: k = 1 gives 1 = 3 + 5 - 7; k = 2 gives 8 = 10 + 12 - 14.

Step 2: Sum over k = 1 to n: 7[n(n + 1)/2] - 6n = (7n^2 - 5n)/2 = n(7n - 5)/2.

Step 3: (ii) Group in threes: (9, 12, -15), (18, 21, -24), ... The k-th group is 9k + (9k + 3) - (9k + 6) = 9k - 3. Check: k = 1 gives 6 = 9 + 12 - 15; k = 2 gives 15 = 18 + 21 - 24.

Step 4: Sum over k = 1 to n: 9[n(n + 1)/2] - 3n = (9n^2 + 3n)/2 = 3n(3n + 1)/2.

Answer: (i) n(7n - 5)/2; (ii) 3n(3n + 1)/2

Worked Example: 4. If S_n = n(2n + 1), then find the series.

Formula used: S_n = (n/2) [2a1 + (n - 1) d] = (n/2) (first term + last term).

Step 1: The n-th term is a_n = S_n - S_{n-1} for n >= 2, and a_1 = S_1.

Step 2: S_1 = 1(3) = 3, so a_1 = 3.

Step 3: S_n - S_{n-1} = (2n^2 + n) - [2(n - 1)^2 + (n - 1)] = (2n^2 + n) - (2n^2 - 3n + 1) = 4n - 1.

Step 4: Hence a_n = 4n - 1: the series is 3 + 7 + 11 + 15 + ... Check: S_3 = 3(7) = 21 = 3 + 7 + 11.

Answer: The series is 3 + 7 + 11 + 15 + ... (a_n = 4n - 1)

Worked Example: 5. Find the sum of first 600 natural numbers which are neither divisible by 2 nor by 5.

Formula used: S_n = (n/2) [2a1 + (n - 1) d] = (n/2) (first term + last term).

Step 1: Among 1 to 600, the numbers neither divisible by 2 nor by 5 are the odd numbers not divisible by 5.

Step 2: Odd numbers from 1 to 600: 300 numbers, their sum = 300^2 = 90000 (sum of the first 300 odd numbers).

Step 3: Odd multiples of 5 among them: 5, 15, ..., 595, which are 60 numbers; their sum = 5(1 + 3 + ... + 119) = 5(60^2) = 18000.

Step 4: Required sum = 90000 - 18000 = 72000. Cross-check by inclusion-exclusion: 180300 - 90300 - 36300 + 18300 = 72000.

Answer: 72000

Worked Example: 7. The sums of n terms of two arithmetic series are in the ratio of 4n - 3 : 2n + 1. Find the ratio of their 7th terms.

Formula used: S_n = (n/2) [2a1 + (n - 1) d] = (n/2) (first term + last term).

Step 1: For an A.P., the sum of the first (2m - 1) terms equals (2m - 1) times the m-th term, so the ratio of the m-th terms equals the ratio of the sums of (2m - 1) terms.

Step 2: For m = 7: 2m - 1 = 13. Ratio of 7th terms = [4(13) - 3] : [2(13) + 1] = 49 : 27.

Answer: 49 : 27

mcqs.q: Sum the series 3 + 7 + 11 + ... up to the 15th term.
Sum the series 4.57 + 4.87 + 5.17 + ... up to the 24th term.
Sum to n terms: 3/sqrt(2) + 2 sqrt(2) + 5/sqrt(2) + ...
mcqs.why: a = 3/sqrt(2), d = 1/sqrt(2). S_n = (n/2)[6/sqrt(2) + (n - 1)/sqrt(2)] = n(n + 5)/(2 sqrt(2)), which rationalises to n(n + 5) sqrt(2)/4.

mcqs.q: Sum the series 2/sqrt(3) + sqrt(3) + 4/sqrt(3) + ... up to the 20th term.
Sum to n terms: (y - 3b) + (y - b) + (y + b) + ...
If S_n = n(2n + 1), what is the n-th term a_n of the series?
Find the sum of the first 600 natural numbers which are neither divisible by 2 nor by 5.
mcqs.why: Odd numbers 1 to 600: 300 numbers with sum 300^2 = 90000. Odd multiples of 5 among them: 60 numbers with sum 5(60^2) = 18000. Required sum = 90000 - 18000 = 72000.

mcqs.q: The sums of n terms of two arithmetic series are in the ratio (4n - 3) : (2n + 1). Find the ratio of their 7th terms.
mcqs.why: The ratio of the m-th terms equals the ratio of the sums of (2m - 1) terms. For m = 7, 2m - 1 = 13: ratio = [4(13) - 3] : [2(13) + 1] = 49 : 27.

mcqs.q: Sum the series 3 + 5 - 7 + 10 + 12 - 14 + 17 + 19 - 21 + ... to 3n terms.
mcqs.why: Group in threes: the k-th group (7k - 4) + (7k - 2) + (-7k) = 7k - 6. Summing k = 1 to n: 7[n(n + 1)/2] - 6n = (7n^2 - 5n)/2 = n(7n - 5)/2.
Group in threes: the k-th group 9k + (9k + 3) - (9k + 6) = 9k - 3. Summing k = 1 to n: 9[n(n + 1)/2] - 3n = (9n^2 + 3n)/2 = 3n(3n + 1)/2.

lessons.title: Exercise 3.4 (p.106) - Geometric Sequences and the n-th Term
lessons.notes_html:
Finding terms of a G.P. from a_n = a1 r^(n - 1): divide two known terms to get a power of r. One question proves that the reciprocals of a G.P.’s terms again form a G.P.

In this exercise: 1. Find the indicated terms of the following G.P. 2. In a G.P., a_1 = 5/9, a_6 = 15625/9. Find its n-th term. 3. Find the n-th term of the geometric sequence if a_7/a_9 = 16/9 and a_2 = 9/4. 4. Show that the reciprocals of the terms of the G.P. 1/a_1, 1/(a_1 r^2), 1/(a_1 r^4), ... form another G.P. Also find the common ratio of the new G.P. 5. How many terms are in G.P. 1/3, 1/12, 1/48, ..., 1/196608. 6. If 1/(xy), 1/(yz), 1/(zx) are in G.P., show that x = +- √(yz).

Worked Example: 1. Find the indicated terms of the following G.P. (i) 2, 6, 18, ..., a7; (ii) 1 + i, 2(1 - i), ..., a10; (iii) 4, 2 √(2), 2, ..., a15; (iv) a^2 - b^2, a + b, (a + b)/(a - b), ..., a9.

Formula used: a_n = a1 r^(n - 1); a_m / a_n = r^(m - n).

Step 1: Use a_n = a_1 r^{n-1}.

Step 2: (i) a_1 = 2, r = 3. a_7 = 2(3^6) = 2(729) = 1458.

Step 3: (ii) a_1 = 1 + i, r = 2(1 - i)/(1 + i) = (1 - i)^2 = -2i. (-2i)^9 = (-2)^9 i^9 = -512i. So a_10 = (1 + i)(-512i) = -512i + 512 = 512 - 512i.

Step 4: (iii) a_1 = 4, r = (2 √(2))/4 = 1/√(2). a_15 = 4(1/√(2))^{14} = 4/2^7 = 4/128 = 1/32.

Step 5: (iv) a_1 = a^2 - b^2, r = (a + b)/(a^2 - b^2) = 1/(a - b). a_9 = (a^2 - b^2)(1/(a - b))^8 = (a - b)(a + b)/(a - b)^8 = (a + b)/(a - b)^7.

Answer: (i) 1458; (ii) 512 - 512i; (iii) 1/32; (iv) (a + b)/(a - b)^7

Worked Example: 3. Find the n-th term of the geometric sequence if a_7/a_9 = 16/9 and a_2 = 9/4.

Formula used: a_n = a1 r^(n - 1); a_m / a_n = r^(m - n).

Step 1: a_7/a_9 = 1/r^2 = 16/9, so r^2 = 9/16 and r = 3/4 or r = -3/4.

Step 2: a_2 = a_1 r = 9/4. If r = 3/4, then a_1 = 3 and a_n = 3(3/4)^{n-1}. If r = -3/4, then a_1 = -3 and a_n = -3(-3/4)^{n-1}. Both satisfy the given data.

Answer: a_n = 3(3/4)^{n-1} or a_n = -3(-3/4)^{n-1}

Worked Example: 4. Show that the reciprocals of the terms of the G.P. 1/a_1, 1/(a_1 r^2), 1/(a_1 r^4), ... form another G.P. Also find the common ratio of the new G.P.

Formula used: a_n = a1 r^(n - 1); a_m / a_n = r^(m - n).

Step 1: The reciprocals of the terms are: 1/(1/a_1) = a_1; 1/(1/(a_1 r^2)) = a_1 r^2; 1/(1/(a_1 r^4)) = a_1 r^4; and so on.

Step 2: Each term divided by the previous one gives (a_1 r^2)/a_1 = r^2 and (a_1 r^4)/(a_1 r^2) = r^2, a constant.

Step 3: Hence the reciprocals form a G.P. with first term a_1 and common ratio r^2.

Answer: The reciprocals form a G.P. with common ratio r^2

Worked Example: 6. If 1/(xy), 1/(yz), 1/(zx) are in G.P., show that x = +- √(yz).

Formula used: a_n = a1 r^(n - 1); a_m / a_n = r^(m - n).

Step 1: In a G.P., the square of the middle term equals the product of the neighbouring terms: (1/(yz))^2 = (1/(xy))(1/(zx)).

Step 2: So 1/(y^2 z^2) = 1/(x^2 y z). Cross-multiplying: x^2 y z = y^2 z^2.

Step 3: Divide by yz (non-zero): x^2 = yz, so x = +- √(yz).

Answer: x = +- √(yz) is proved

mcqs.q: Find the 7th term of the G.P. 2, 6, 18, ...
Find the 15th term of the G.P. 4, 2 sqrt(2), 2, ...
Find the 10th term of the G.P. 1 + i, 2(1 - i), ...
Find the 9th term of the G.P. a^2 - b^2, a + b, (a + b)/(a - b), ...
In a G.P., a_1 = 5/9 and a_6 = 15625/9. What is the common ratio r?
In a G.P., a_1 = 5/9 and a_6 = 15625/9. What is the n-th term?
For a geometric sequence, a_7/a_9 = 16/9. What is r^2?
How many terms are in the G.P. 1/3, 1/12, 1/48, ..., 1/196608?
The reciprocals of the terms of the G.P. 1/a_1, 1/(a_1 r^2), 1/(a_1 r^4), ... form another G.P. What is its common ratio?
mcqs.why: The reciprocals are a_1, a_1 r^2, a_1 r^4, ... and each divided by the previous gives (a_1 r^2)/a_1 = r^2, a constant, so the new G.P. has common ratio r^2.

mcqs.q: If 1/(xy), 1/(yz), 1/(zx) are in G.P., what does the G.P. condition give for x?
options: x = sqrt(yz) only, with no sign choice
mcqs.why: In a G.P. the middle term squared equals the product of its neighbours: (1/(yz))^2 = (1/(xy))(1/(zx)), so 1/(y^2 z^2) = 1/(x^2 y z), giving x^2 = yz and x = +/- sqrt(yz).

lessons.title: Exercise 3.5 (p.109) - Geometric Means
lessons.notes_html:
The G.M. between two numbers is the square root of their product (same sign); inserting n G.Ms. builds a G.P. with r = (b / a)^(1 / (n + 1)). One question links the A.M. and G.M. of two numbers back to the numbers themselves.

In this exercise: 1. Find G.M. between. 2. Insert two G.Ms. between 3 and 81. 3. Insert five G.Ms. between 16 and 1024. 4. Insert six G.Ms. between 9 and 19683. 5. The A.M. between two numbers is 17 and the geometric mean is 15, find the numbers. 6. For what value of n, is (x^{n-2} + y^{n-2})/(x^{n-3} + y^{n-3}) the G.M. between x and y. 7. Show that the n-th root of the product of n geometric means between a and b is the geometric mean between a and b.

Worked Example: 1. Find G.M. between: (i) 4 and 9; (ii) 4 √(5) and 5 √(5); (iii) 5 + i and 5 - i; (iv) 16/9 and 9/25.

Formula used: G.M. = √(a b) (for positive a, b); n means between a and b: r = (b / a)^(1 / (n + 1)).

Step 1: The geometric mean between a and b is G = +- √(ab).

Step 2: (i) +- √(4 x 9) = +- √(36) = +-6.

Step 3: (ii) +- √(4 √(5) x 5 √(5)) = +- √(100) = +-10.

Step 4: (iii) +- √((5 + i)(5 - i)) = +- √(26).

Step 5: (iv) +- √((16/9)(9/25)) = +- √(16/25) = +-4/5.

Answer: (i) +-6; (ii) +-10; (iii) +-√(26); (iv) +-4/5

Worked Example: 3. Insert five G.Ms. between 16 and 1024.

Formula used: G.M. = √(a b) (for positive a, b); n means between a and b: r = (b / a)^(1 / (n + 1)).

Step 1: Inserting five means gives 7 terms in G.P.: first term 16, seventh term 1024.

Step 2: So 16r^6 = 1024, r^6 = 64, r = 2 or r = -2.

Step 3: With r = 2 the means are 32, 64, 128, 256, 512. With r = -2 they are -32, 64, -128, 256, -512. (The book's worked example uses the positive root.)

Answer: With r = 2: 32, 64, 128, 256, 512; with r = -2: -32, 64, -128, 256, -512

Worked Example: 4. Insert six G.Ms. between 9 and 19683.

Formula used: G.M. = √(a b) (for positive a, b); n means between a and b: r = (b / a)^(1 / (n + 1)).

Step 1: Inserting six means gives 8 terms in G.P.: first term 9, eighth term 19683.

Step 2: So 9r^7 = 19683, r^7 = 2187 = 3^7, r = 3.

Step 3: The six means are 27, 81, 243, 729, 2187, 6561.

Answer: 27, 81, 243, 729, 2187, 6561

Worked Example: 5. The A.M. between two numbers is 17 and the geometric mean is 15, find the numbers.

Formula used: G.M. = √(a b) (for positive a, b); n means between a and b: r = (b / a)^(1 / (n + 1)).

Step 1: Let the numbers be a and b. Then (a + b)/2 = 17, so a + b = 34; and √(ab) = 15, so ab = 225.

Step 2: Thus a and b are the roots of t^2 - 34t + 225 = 0.

Step 3: Discriminant = 34^2 - 4(225) = 1156 - 900 = 256 = 16^2. So t = (34 +- 16)/2 = 25 or 9.

Step 4: The numbers are 25 and 9.

Answer: 25 and 9

Worked Example: 7. Show that the n-th root of the product of n geometric means between a and b is the geometric mean between a and b.

Formula used: G.M. = √(a b) (for positive a, b); n means between a and b: r = (b / a)^(1 / (n + 1)).

Step 1: Let G_1, ..., G_n be the n geometric means between a and b. Then a, G_1, ..., G_n, b are in G.P. with n + 2 terms.

Step 2: Let r be the common ratio: b = a r^{n+1}, so r^{n+1} = b/a, and G_k = a r^k.

Step 3: The product G_1 ... G_n = (a r)(a r^2)...(a r^n) = a^n r^{1+2+...+n} = a^n r^{n(n+1)/2}.

Step 4: Its n-th root is a r^{(n+1)/2} = a (r^{n+1})^{1/2} = a (b/a)^{1/2} = √(ab), which is the geometric mean between a and b.

Answer: The n-th root of the product is √(ab), the G.M. between a and b

mcqs.q: Find the G.M. between 4 and 9.
mcqs.why: G.M. = +/- sqrt(ab) = +/- sqrt(4 x 9) = +/- sqrt(36), i.e. 6 and -6.

mcqs.q: Find the G.M. between 4 sqrt(5) and 5 sqrt(5).
mcqs.why: G.M. = +/- sqrt(ab) = +/- sqrt(4 sqrt(5) x 5 sqrt(5)) = +/- sqrt(100), i.e. 10 and -10.

mcqs.q: Find the G.M. between 5 + i and 5 - i.
Find the G.M. between 16/9 and 9/25.
Insert two G.Ms. between 3 and 81. What are the two means (taking the positive ratio)?
mcqs.why: Four terms in G.P.: 3 r^3 = 81 gives r^3 = 27, r = 3. The means are 3(3) = 9 and 3(3^2) = 27.

mcqs.q: Insert five G.Ms. between 16 and 1024. What is the common ratio (positive value)?
mcqs.why: Seven terms in G.P.: 16 r^6 = 1024 gives r^6 = 64 = 2^6, so r = 2 (the notes also note r = -2 is possible).

mcqs.q: Insert five G.Ms. between 16 and 1024 with r = 2. What is the first mean?
mcqs.why: With r = 2 from 16 r^6 = 1024, the means are 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, so the first mean is 16 x 2 = 32.

mcqs.q: Insert six G.Ms. between 9 and 19683. What is the first mean?
mcqs.why: Eight terms in G.P.: 9 r^7 = 19683 gives r^7 = 2187 = 3^7, r = 3. The first mean is 9 x 3 = 27 (the means are 27, 81, 243, 729, 2187, 6561).

mcqs.q: The A.M. between two numbers is 17 and the G.M. is 15. Find the numbers.
mcqs.why: a + b = 2(17) = 34 and ab = 15^2 = 225. The numbers are roots of t^2 - 34t + 225 = 0; discriminant 1156 - 900 = 256, t = (34 +/- 16)/2 = 25 or 9. The numbers are 25 and 9.

mcqs.q: The n-th root of the product of the n geometric means between a and b equals what?
options: sqrt(ab), the G.M. between a and b
(a + b)/2, the A.M. between a and b
ab, the product of a and b
2ab/(a + b), the H.M. between a and b
mcqs.why: With G_k = a r^k and r^(n+1) = b/a, the product is a^n r^(n(n+1)/2); its n-th root is a r^((n+1)/2) = a (b/a)^(1/2) = sqrt(ab), the G.M. between a and b.

lessons.title: Exercise 3.6 (pp.114-115) - Sum of a Geometric Series and Recurring Decimals
lessons.notes_html:
Summing finite and infinite G.Ps. An infinite sum exists only when |r| < 1, and that is exactly what turns a recurring decimal into a vulgar fraction. The last questions reverse the process: from a given sum, find the series.

In this exercise: 1. Compute the sum. 2. Sum to n terms, the series. 3. If a_n = (1/4)^n then find its sum up to n terms. 4. Find the sums of the following infinite geometric series. 5. Find the vulgar fraction equivalent to the following recurring decimals (dots verified at 300 dpi: the repetend is the block under the dots). 6. If x = y/2 + y^2/4 + y^3/8 + ... if 0 < y < 2, prove that y = 2x/(1 + x). 7. If x = 3y/2 + 9y^2/4 + 27y^3/8 + ... if 0 < y < 2/3, then prove that y = 2x/[3(1 + x)]. 8. The sum of an infinite geometric series is one third the sum of the squares of its terms. If the sum of its first two terms is 3/4, find the series.

Worked Example: 1. Compute the sum. (i) 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + ... + 1/512; (ii) 2^6 + 2^7 + 2^8 + ... + 2^13; (iii) 1/u + 1/u^2 + 1/u^3 + ... + 1/u^8; (iv) 9 + 3 + 1 + ... + 1/2187; (v) 0.9 + 0.99 + 0.999 + ... to n terms; (vi) 7 + 77 + 777 + ... to n terms.

Formula used: S_n = a1 (r^n - 1) / (r - 1); S_inf = a1 / (1 - r) when |r| < 1; recurring block of length k gives ratio 1 / 10^k.

Step 1: Use S_n = a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r) for r different from 1.

Step 2: (i) a = 1, r = 1/2, n = 10 (since 1/512 = (1/2)^9 is the 10th term). S = (1 - (1/2)^10)/(1/2) = 2(1 - 1/1024) = 1023/512.

Step 3: (ii) a = 64, r = 2, n = 8. S = 64(2^8 - 1)/(2 - 1) = 64(255) = 16320.

Step 4: (iii) a = 1/u, r = 1/u, n = 8. S = (1/u)(1 - u^{-8})/(1 - 1/u) = (u^8 - 1)/(u^8 (u - 1)).

Step 5: (iv) a = 9, r = 1/3. The last term 9(1/3)^{n-1} = 1/2187 = 3^{-7} gives n = 10. S = 9(1 - (1/3)^10)/(2/3) = (27/2)(59048/59049) = 29524/2187.

Step 6: (v) The k-th term is 1 - (1/10)^k. Sum = n - (1/10)(1 - (1/10)^n)/(9/10) = n - (1/9)(1 - 10^{-n}) = n - 1/9 + 10^{-n}/9.

Step 7: (vi) The k-th term is 7(10^k - 1)/9. Sum = (7/9)[10(10^n - 1)/9 - n] = 70(10^n - 1)/81 - 7n/9.

Answer: (i) 1023/512; (ii) 16320; (iii) (u^8 - 1)/(u^8 (u - 1)); (iv) 29524/2187; (v) n - 1/9 + 10^{-n}/9; (vi) 70(10^n - 1)/81 - 7n/9

Worked Example: 3. If a_n = (1/4)^n then find its sum up to n terms.

Formula used: S_n = a1 (r^n - 1) / (r - 1); S_inf = a1 / (1 - r) when |r| < 1; recurring block of length k gives ratio 1 / 10^k.

Step 1: The series is 1/4 + (1/4)^2 + ... + (1/4)^n, a G.P. with a = 1/4, r = 1/4.

Step 2: Sum = (1/4)(1 - (1/4)^n)/(1 - 1/4) = (1/4)(1 - 4^{-n})/(3/4) = (1/3)(1 - 4^{-n}).

Answer: (1/3)(1 - 4^{-n})

Worked Example: 5. Find the vulgar fraction equivalent to the following recurring decimals (dots verified at 300 dpi: the repetend is the block under the dots). (i) 1.5454... (ii) 0.267267... (iii) 1.14848... (iv) 1.6666... (v) 3.26767... (vi) 1.45757...

Formula used: S_n = a1 (r^n - 1) / (r - 1); S_inf = a1 / (1 - r) when |r| < 1; recurring block of length k gives ratio 1 / 10^k.

Step 1: Write each recurring decimal as a geometric series and sum it, or use the standard rule: repetend over as many 9s, with non-repeating part adjusted.

Step 2: (i) 1.5454... = 1 + 54/99 = 1 + 6/11 = 17/11.

Step 3: (ii) 0.267267... = 267/999 = 89/333.

Step 4: (iii) 1.14848... = 1.1 + 48/990 = 11/10 + 8/165 = 379/330.

Step 5: (iv) 1.6666... = 1 + 6/9 = 5/3.

Step 6: (v) 3.26767... = 3.2 + 67/990 = 16/5 + 67/990 = 647/198.

Step 7: (vi) 1.45757... = 1.4 + 57/990 = 7/5 + 57/990 = 481/330.

Answer: (i) 17/11; (ii) 89/333; (iii) 379/330; (iv) 5/3; (v) 647/198; (vi) 481/330

Worked Example: 6. If x = y/2 + y^2/4 + y^3/8 + ... if 0 < y < 2, prove that y = 2x/(1 + x).

Formula used: S_n = a1 (r^n - 1) / (r - 1); S_inf = a1 / (1 - r) when |r| < 1; recurring block of length k gives ratio 1 / 10^k.

Step 1: The series is geometric with first term y/2 and ratio y/2. Since 0 < y < 2, |y/2| < 1, so it converges.

Step 2: Its sum is x = (y/2)/(1 - y/2) = y/(2 - y).

Step 3: Then x(2 - y) = y, i.e. 2x - xy = y, so 2x = y(1 + x), giving y = 2x/(1 + x).

Answer: y = 2x/(1 + x) is proved

Worked Example: 8. The sum of an infinite geometric series is one third the sum of the squares of its terms. If the sum of its first two terms is 3/4, find the series.

Formula used: S_n = a1 (r^n - 1) / (r - 1); S_inf = a1 / (1 - r) when |r| < 1; recurring block of length k gives ratio 1 / 10^k.

Step 1: Let the first term be a and the ratio be r, |r| < 1. Sum of the series = a/(1 - r).

Step 2: The squares form a G.P. with first term a^2 and ratio r^2; their sum = a^2/(1 - r^2).

Step 3: Given: a/(1 - r) = (1/3) a^2/(1 - r^2) = (1/3) a^2/[(1 - r)(1 + r)]. Cancelling a/(1 - r) (non-zero) gives 1 = a/[3(1 + r)], so a = 3(1 + r).

Step 4: Also a + ar = a(1 + r) = 3/4. Substituting a: 3(1 + r)^2 = 3/4, so (1 + r)^2 = 1/4, 1 + r = +-1/2.

Step 5: r = -3/2 is rejected (|r| >= 1, the infinite sum would not exist). Hence r = -1/2 and a = 3(1/2) = 3/2.

Step 6: The series is 3/2 - 3/4 + 3/8 - ... Check: sum = (3/2)/(3/2) = 1, and sum of squares = (9/4)/(3/4) = 3 = 3(1).

Answer: The series is 3/2 - 3/4 + 3/8 - ... (a = 3/2, r = -1/2)

mcqs.q: Compute the sum 9 + 3 + 1 + ... + 1/2187.
If a_n = (1/4)^n, find the sum of the series up to n terms.
Find the vulgar fraction equal to the recurring decimal 1.5454...
mcqs.why: 1.5454... = 1 + 54/99 = 1 + 6/11 = 17/11, using the repetend 54 over two 9s as an infinite G.P. with ratio 1/100.

mcqs.q: Find the vulgar fraction equal to the recurring decimal 0.267267...
mcqs.why: 0.267267... = 267/999 as an infinite G.P. with ratio 1/1000, and 267/999 reduces by dividing by 3 to 89/333.

mcqs.q: Find the vulgar fraction equal to the recurring decimal 1.6666...
mcqs.why: 1.6666... = 1 + 6/9 = 1 + 2/3 = 5/3, using the single repeating digit 6 over one 9.

mcqs.q: Find the vulgar fraction equal to the recurring decimal 1.14848...
Find the vulgar fraction equal to the recurring decimal 3.26767...
An infinite geometric series has a finite sum only under which condition on r?
mcqs.why: The notes give S_inf = a1/(1 - r) when |r| < 1; outside this range the terms do not shrink to zero and no finite infinite sum exists. This is also why r = -3/2 is rejected in the last worked example of the exercise.

lessons.title: Exercise 3.7 (p.117) - Harmonic Sequences and the n-th Term
lessons.notes_html:
An H.P. is handled through its reciprocal A.P.: invert every term, use a_n = a1 + (n - 1)d there, and invert the answer back.

In this exercise: 1. Find the n-th term of the H.P. 2. Find the 10th terms of the following harmonic sequences. 3. If the 7th and 10th terms of a H.P. are 1/3 and 5/21 respectively, find its 20th term. 4. If the numbers 1/u, 1/(2u + 1) and 1/(4u - 1) are in H.P., find u. 5. If the sum of first and sixth terms of H.P. is 31/116, find the sequence if the first term is 1/4. 6. In a harmonic progression, 5th and 9th terms are 7/30 and 7/54 respectively, find the 15th term.

Worked Example: 1. Find the n-th term of the H.P. (i) 1/3, 1/7, 1/11, ... (ii) 9/5, 9/13, 9/21, ...

Formula used: If 1/a_n is in A.P., then a_n is in H.P.; n-th term of the H.P. = 1 / (n-th term of the reciprocal A.P.).

Step 1: For an H.P., the reciprocals of the terms form an A.P.; find the n-th term of that A.P. and take its reciprocal.

Step 2: (i) Reciprocals: 3, 7, 11, ... with a = 3, d = 4. The n-th reciprocal is 3 + (n - 1)(4) = 4n - 1. Hence the n-th term of the H.P. is 1/(4n - 1).

Step 3: (ii) Reciprocals: 5/9, 13/9, 21/9, ... with a = 5/9, d = 8/9. The n-th reciprocal is 5/9 + (n - 1)(8/9) = (8n - 3)/9. Hence the n-th term of the H.P. is 9/(8n - 3).

Answer: (i) 1/(4n - 1); (ii) 9/(8n - 3)

Worked Example: 3. If the 7th and 10th terms of a H.P. are 1/3 and 5/21 respectively, find its 20th term.

Formula used: If 1/a_n is in A.P., then a_n is in H.P.; n-th term of the H.P. = 1 / (n-th term of the reciprocal A.P.).

Step 1: Work with reciprocals, which form an A.P. The 7th reciprocal is 3 and the 10th reciprocal is 21/5.

Step 2: Let the A.P. have first term a and difference d: a + 6d = 3 and a + 9d = 21/5.

Step 3: Subtracting: 3d = 21/5 - 3 = 6/5, so d = 2/5. Then a = 3 - 6(2/5) = 3/5.

Step 4: The 20th reciprocal is 3/5 + 19(2/5) = 41/5. Hence the 20th term of the H.P. is 5/41.

Answer: 5/41

Worked Example: 4. If the numbers 1/u, 1/(2u + 1) and 1/(4u - 1) are in H.P., find u.

Formula used: If 1/a_n is in A.P., then a_n is in H.P.; n-th term of the H.P. = 1 / (n-th term of the reciprocal A.P.).

Step 1: The reciprocals u, 2u + 1, 4u - 1 must be in A.P.

Step 2: So twice the middle term equals the sum of the extremes: 2(2u + 1) = u + (4u - 1).

Step 3: Thus 4u + 2 = 5u - 1, giving u = 3.

Answer: u = 3

Worked Example: 6. In a harmonic progression, 5th and 9th terms are 7/30 and 7/54 respectively, find the 15th term.

Formula used: If 1/a_n is in A.P., then a_n is in H.P.; n-th term of the H.P. = 1 / (n-th term of the reciprocal A.P.).

Step 1: Work with reciprocals: the 5th reciprocal is 30/7 and the 9th reciprocal is 54/7.

Step 2: Let the A.P. have first term a and difference d: a + 4d = 30/7 and a + 8d = 54/7.

Step 3: Subtracting: 4d = 24/7, so d = 6/7. Then a = 30/7 - 4(6/7) = 6/7.

Step 4: The 15th reciprocal is 6/7 + 14(6/7) = 90/7. Hence the 15th term of the H.P. is 7/90.

Answer: 7/90

mcqs.q: Find the n-th term of the H.P. 1/3, 1/7, 1/11, ...
mcqs.why: Reciprocals 3, 7, 11, ... form an A.P. with a = 3, d = 4; its n-th term is 3 + (n - 1)(4) = 4n - 1. Inverting gives the H.P. n-th term 1/(4n - 1).

mcqs.q: Find the n-th term of the H.P. 9/5, 9/13, 9/21, ...
mcqs.why: Reciprocals 5/9, 13/9, 21/9, ... form an A.P. with a = 5/9, d = 8/9; its n-th term is (8n - 3)/9. Inverting gives the H.P. n-th term 9/(8n - 3).

mcqs.q: The 7th and 10th terms of an H.P. are 1/3 and 5/21. Find its 20th term.
mcqs.why: Reciprocals form an A.P.: a + 6d = 3, a + 9d = 21/5. Subtracting: 3d = 6/5, d = 2/5, a = 3/5. The 20th reciprocal is 3/5 + 19(2/5) = 41/5, so the 20th H.P. term is 5/41.

mcqs.q: The 7th and 10th terms of an H.P. are 1/3 and 5/21. What is d, the difference of the reciprocal A.P.?
mcqs.why: Reciprocals: a + 6d = 3 and a + 9d = 21/5. Subtracting gives 3d = 21/5 - 3 = 6/5, so d = 2/5.

mcqs.q: If 1/u, 1/(2u + 1) and 1/(4u - 1) are in H.P., find u.
mcqs.why: The reciprocals u, 2u + 1, 4u - 1 must be in A.P., so 2(2u + 1) = u + (4u - 1), i.e. 4u + 2 = 5u - 1, giving u = 3.

mcqs.q: In an H.P., the 5th and 9th terms are 7/30 and 7/54. Find the 15th term.
mcqs.why: Reciprocals: a + 4d = 30/7, a + 8d = 54/7. Subtracting: 4d = 24/7, d = 6/7, a = 6/7. The 15th reciprocal is 6/7 + 14(6/7) = 90/7, so the 15th H.P. term is 7/90.

mcqs.q: To solve an H.P. problem, what is the standard first step given in this exercise?
options: Multiply every term by the first term
Invert every term to get an A.P., solve there, then invert back
Add the reciprocals of the end terms
Square every term to get a G.P.
mcqs.why: The exercise method is: for an H.P., the reciprocals of the terms form an A.P.; find the required term of that A.P. and take its reciprocal.

mcqs.q: Using the H.P. 1/3, 1/7, 1/11, ... of this exercise, find its 10th term.
mcqs.why: The n-th term is 1/(4n - 1) from the reciprocal A.P. 3, 7, 11, ... Substituting n = 10: 1/(40 - 1) = 1/39.

mcqs.q: An H.P. has 7th term 1/3 and 10th term 5/21 (reciprocal A.P. first term 3/5). What is the first term of the H.P.?
mcqs.why: The reciprocal A.P. has a = 3/5 (from a + 6d = 3 with d = 2/5: a = 3 - 12/5 = 3/5). The first H.P. term is the reciprocal of this: 1/(3/5) = 5/3.

mcqs.q: The sum of the first and sixth terms of an H.P. is 31/116 and the first term is 1/4. Find the sixth term.
mcqs.why: Sixth term = 31/116 - 1/4 = 31/116 - 29/116 = 2/116 = 1/58, directly from the given sum and the first term 1/4 = 29/116.

lessons.title: Exercise 3.8 (p.122) - Harmonic Means and the Three Means
lessons.notes_html:
The H.M. between a and b is 2ab / (a + b) — the reciprocal of the A.M. of the reciprocals. Inserting H.Ms. is done in the reciprocal A.P., and the final question checks G^2 = A x H.

In this exercise: 1. Find H.Ms. between the following numbers. 2. Insert four H.Ms. between 1/9 and 1/81. 3. Insert six H.Ms. between 1/12 and 1/48. 4. Find n so that (a^{n-5} + b^{n-5})/(a^{n-6} + b^{n-6}) may be H.M. between a and b. 5. Find A, G and H and show that G^2 = A x H, if.

Worked Example: 1. Find H.Ms. between the following numbers. (i) 4 and 9; (ii) 3 + √(2) and 3 - √(2); (iii) 2 + 3i and 2 - 3i; (iv) 1/7 and 1/11.

Formula used: H.M. = 2ab / (a + b); A = (a + b) / 2; G = √(a b); G^2 = A x H.

Step 1: The harmonic mean between a and b is H = 2ab/(a + b).

Step 2: (i) 2(4)(9)/(4 + 9) = 72/13.

Step 3: (ii) ab = (3 + √(2))(3 - √(2)) = 7, a + b = 6. H = 2(7)/6 = 7/3.

Step 4: (iii) ab = (2 + 3i)(2 - 3i) = 13, a + b = 4. H = 2(13)/4 = 13/2.

Step 5: (iv) ab = 1/77, a + b = 18/77. H = 2(1/77)/(18/77) = 2/18 = 1/9.

Answer: (i) 72/13; (ii) 7/3; (iii) 13/2; (iv) 1/9

Worked Example: 2. Insert four H.Ms. between 1/9 and 1/81.

Formula used: H.M. = 2ab / (a + b); A = (a + b) / 2; G = √(a b); G^2 = A x H.

Step 1: Work with reciprocals: they form an A.P. with 6 terms, first term 9, sixth term 81.

Step 2: Let the difference be d: 9 + 5d = 81, so d = 72/5.

Step 3: The reciprocals of the four means are 9 + 72/5 = 117/5, 189/5, 261/5, 333/5.

Step 4: Taking reciprocals, the four H.Ms. are 5/117, 5/189, 5/261, 5/333.

Answer: 5/117, 5/189, 5/261, 5/333

Worked Example: 4. Find n so that (a^{n-5} + b^{n-5})/(a^{n-6} + b^{n-6}) may be H.M. between a and b.

Formula used: H.M. = 2ab / (a + b); A = (a + b) / 2; G = √(a b); G^2 = A x H.

Step 1: The H.M. between a and b is 2ab/(a + b). Put m = n - 6, so the expression is (a^{m+1} + b^{m+1})/(a^m + b^m).

Step 2: Set it equal to 2ab/(a + b) and cross-multiply: (a + b)(a^{m+1} + b^{m+1}) = 2ab(a^m + b^m).

Step 3: Expand: a^{m+2} + a b^{m+1} + a^{m+1} b + b^{m+2} = 2a^{m+1} b + 2a b^{m+1}.

Step 4: Rearrange: a^{m+2} - a^{m+1} b - a b^{m+1} + b^{m+2} = (a - b)(a^{m+1} - b^{m+1}) = 0.

Step 5: For a different from b this holds identically only when m + 1 = 0, i.e. m = -1. Hence n = 5.

Step 6: Check: for n = 5 the expression is (1 + 1)/(1/a + 1/b) = 2ab/(a + b).

Answer: n = 5

Worked Example: 5. Find A, G and H and show that G^2 = A x H, if (i) a = 12, b = 3; (ii) a = 2/5, b = 8/5.

Formula used: H.M. = 2ab / (a + b); A = (a + b) / 2; G = √(a b); G^2 = A x H.

Step 1: Use A = (a + b)/2, G = √(ab), H = 2ab/(a + b).

Step 2: (i) A = (12 + 3)/2 = 15/2; G = √(36) = 6; H = 2(36)/15 = 24/5. Then A x H = (15/2)(24/5) = 36 = G^2.

Step 3: (ii) A = (2/5 + 8/5)/2 = 1; G = √(16/25) = 4/5; H = 2(16/25)/(10/5) = 16/25. Then A x H = 16/25 = G^2.

Answer: (i) A = 15/2, G = 6, H = 24/5, and G^2 = A x H = 36; (ii) A = 1, G = 4/5, H = 16/25, and G^2 = A x H = 16/25

mcqs.q: Find the H.M. between 4 and 9.
Find the H.M. between 3 + sqrt(2) and 3 - sqrt(2).
Find the H.M. between 2 + 3i and 2 - 3i.
Find the H.M. between 1/7 and 1/11.
Insert four H.Ms. between 1/9 and 1/81. What is the first of the four means?
mcqs.why: Reciprocals form an A.P. of 6 terms: 9 + 5d = 81 gives d = 72/5. The first mean's reciprocal is 9 + 72/5 = 117/5, so the first H.M. is 5/117 (the four are 5/117, 5/189, 5/261, 5/333).

mcqs.q: Insert six H.Ms. between 1/12 and 1/48. What is the first of the six means?
mcqs.why: Reciprocals form an A.P. of 8 terms: 12 + 7d = 48 gives d = 36/7. The first mean's reciprocal is 12 + 36/7 = 120/7, so the first H.M. is 7/120.

mcqs.q: Find n so that (a^(n-5) + b^(n-5))/(a^(n-6) + b^(n-6)) may be the H.M. between a and b.
mcqs.why: Setting the expression equal to 2ab/(a + b) and simplifying gives (a - b)(a^(m+1) - b^(m+1)) = 0 with m = n - 6, which holds identically only for m = -1. Hence n = 5; check: the expression becomes (1 + 1)/(1/a + 1/b) = 2ab/(a + b).

mcqs.q: For a = 12 and b = 3, find the harmonic mean H.
mcqs.why: H = 2ab/(a + b) = 2(12)(3)/(12 + 3) = 72/15 = 24/5. (For reference A = 15/2 and G = 6 in this case.)

mcqs.q: For a = 2/5 and b = 8/5, find the harmonic mean H.
mcqs.why: H = 2ab/(a + b) = 2(16/25)/(10/5) = (32/25)/2 = 16/25. (For reference A = 1 and G = 4/5 in this case.)

mcqs.q: For a = 12 and b = 3, A = 15/2, G = 6 and H = 24/5. What is the value of both G^2 and A x H?
mcqs.why: G^2 = 6^2 = 36 and A x H = (15/2)(24/5) = 360/10 = 36, confirming G^2 = A x H for these numbers.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 3 (pp.122-123)
lessons.notes_html:
Review of Unit 3: A.P., G.P. and H.P. terms and sums, inserted means, and problems mixing the three means.

In this exercise: 1. Choose the correct options. 2. The 8th term of an arithmetic sequence is 75 and 20th term is 39. Find 24th term. 3. There are n A.Ms. between 5 and 32 such that the ratio of the third and 7th means is 7:13, find the value of n. 4. Find the sum of all the integers between 450 and 750 which are divisible by 7. 5. How many terms are there if a_1 = 4, a_n = 1/256, r = 1/2. 6. The yearly depreciation of a certain machine is 15% of the value at the beginning of the year. If the original cost of the machine is Rs 4,000, find the value after 4 years. 7. Find r if S_10 = 244 S_5, for a geometric series. 8. If A.M. and H.M. between two numbers are 5 and 4 1/5 respectively, find the numbers. 9. If G.M. and H.M. between two numbers are 15 and 5 10/13 respectively, find the numbers. 10. The second term of an H.P. is 1/2 and the fifth term is -1/4. Find the 12th term.

Worked Example: 1(i). If the difference between two consecutive terms is same then the sequence is called;

a) arithmetic   b) geometric   c) harmonic   d) none of these

Answer: a) arithmetic

Worked Example: 1(ii). 3, 6, 12, ... are G.P. then its 6th term is;

a) 24   b) 48   c) 96   d) 192

Answer: c) 96

Worked Example: 1(iii). G.M. between 4 and 16 is;

a) 2   b) 4   c) 96   d) 8

Answer: d) 8

Worked Example: 1(iv). If the reciprocal of the terms of sequence are in arithmetic progression then sequence is known as;

a) arithmetic   b) geometric   c) harmonic   d) none of these

Answer: c) harmonic

Worked Example: 1(v). n-th term of A.P. is a_n =

a) a_1 + (n - 1)d   b) a_1 r^{n-1}   c) 1/(a_1 + (n - 1)d)   d) (a_1 + (n - 1)d)/(a_1 r^{n-1})

Answer: a) a_1 + (n - 1)d

Worked Example: 1(vi). If a = 9, b = 11 then A.M. =

a) 5   b) 10   c) 15   d) 20

Answer: b) 10

Worked Example: 1(vii). If (2/3)^3, (5/3)^3, (8/3)^3, ... are in A.P. then its nth term is

a) ((5n - 1)/3)^3   b) ((4n - 1)/3)^3   c) ((3n - 1)/3)^3   d) ((2n - 1)/3)^3

Answer: c) ((3n - 1)/3)^3

Worked Example: 1(viii). If a = 4 - 3i, b = 4 + 3i then G.M. is;

a) 20   b) 15   c) 10   d) 5

Answer: d) 5

Worked Example: 1(ix). 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + 100 is;

a) 5000   b) 5050   c) 5100   d) 5150

Answer: b) 5050

Worked Example: 2. The 8th term of an arithmetic sequence is 75 and 20th term is 39. Find 24th term.

Formula used: See the formulas in the Unit 3 Overview and Lessons 1 to 8 of this unit.

Step 1: Let the first term be a and the difference be d: a + 7d = 75 and a + 19d = 39.

Step 2: Subtracting: 12d = -36, so d = -3. Then a = 75 - 7(-3) = 96.

Step 3: The 24th term is a + 23d = 96 + 23(-3) = 96 - 69 = 27.

Answer: 27

Worked Example: 4. Find the sum of all the integers between 450 and 750 which are divisible by 7.

Formula used: See the formulas in the Unit 3 Overview and Lessons 1 to 8 of this unit.

Step 1: The first such integer is 455 = 7 x 65 and the last is 749 = 7 x 107.

Step 2: The count is 107 - 65 + 1 = 43 terms, in A.P. with difference 7.

Step 3: Sum = (43/2)(455 + 749) = (43/2)(1204) = 43 x 602 = 25886.

Answer: 25886

Worked Example: 6. The yearly depreciation of a certain machine is 15% of the value at the beginning of the year. If the original cost of the machine is Rs 4,000, find the value after 4 years.

Formula used: See the formulas in the Unit 3 Overview and Lessons 1 to 8 of this unit.

Step 1: Each year the value is multiplied by 1 - 0.15 = 0.85, a G.P. with ratio 0.85.

Step 2: Value after 4 years = 4000 x (0.85)^4 = 4000 x 0.52200625 = 2088.025, i.e. about Rs 2088.03.

Answer: Rs 2088.03 (approximately)

Worked Example: 8. If A.M. and H.M. between two numbers are 5 and 4 1/5 respectively, find the numbers.

Formula used: See the formulas in the Unit 3 Overview and Lessons 1 to 8 of this unit.

Step 1: Let the numbers be a and b. Then (a + b)/2 = 5, so a + b = 10.

Step 2: Also 2ab/(a + b) = 21/5, so 2ab/10 = 21/5, giving ab = 21.

Step 3: Thus a and b are the roots of t^2 - 10t + 21 = 0, i.e. (t - 3)(t - 7) = 0. The numbers are 3 and 7.

Answer: 3 and 7

Worked Example: 10. The second term of an H.P. is 1/2 and the fifth term is -1/4. Find the 12th term.

Formula used: See the formulas in the Unit 3 Overview and Lessons 1 to 8 of this unit.

Step 1: Work with reciprocals, which form an A.P. The 2nd reciprocal is 2 and the 5th reciprocal is -4.

Step 2: Let the A.P. have first term a and difference d: a + d = 2 and a + 4d = -4.

Step 3: Subtracting: 3d = -6, so d = -2 and a = 4.

Step 4: The 12th reciprocal is 4 + 11(-2) = -18. Hence the 12th term of the H.P. is -1/18.

Answer: -1/18

mcqs.q: In the G.P. 3, 6, 12, ..., what is the 6th term?
mcqs.why: a_n = a1 r^(n - 1) with a1 = 3, r = 2. a_6 = 3(2^5) = 3(32) = 96. This is item (ii) of the review multiple-choice set.

mcqs.q: The 8th term of an arithmetic sequence is 75 and the 20th term is 39. Find the 24th term.
There are n A.Ms. between 5 and 32 such that the ratio of the third and 7th means is 7 : 13. Find n.
Find the sum of all integers between 450 and 750 which are divisible by 7.
A G.P. has a_1 = 4, a_n = 1/256 and r = 1/2. How many terms are there?
A machine costing Rs 4,000 depreciates 15% of its value each year. Find its value after 4 years (approximately).
mcqs.why: Each year the value is multiplied by 1 - 0.15 = 0.85, a G.P. with ratio 0.85. Value after 4 years = 4000 x (0.85)^4 = 4000 x 0.52200625 = 2088.025, about Rs 2088.03.

mcqs.q: For a geometric series, S_10 = 244 S_5. Find the common ratio r.
The A.M. and H.M. between two numbers are 5 and 4 1/5 respectively. Find the numbers.
mcqs.why: a + b = 2(5) = 10 and 2ab/(a + b) = 21/5 gives 2ab/10 = 21/5, so ab = 21. The numbers are roots of t^2 - 10t + 21 = 0 = (t - 3)(t - 7): the numbers are 3 and 7.

mcqs.q: The G.M. and H.M. between two numbers are 15 and 5 10/13 respectively. Find the numbers.
mcqs.why: ab = 15^2 = 225 and H = 2ab/(a + b) = 75/13 gives a + b = 450 x 13/75 = 78. The numbers are roots of t^2 - 78t + 225 = 0; discriminant 6084 - 900 = 5184 = 72^2, t = (78 +/- 72)/2 = 75 or 3. The numbers are 75 and 3.

mcqs.q: The second term of an H.P. is 1/2 and the fifth term is -1/4. Find the 12th term.
mcqs.why: Reciprocals form an A.P.: a + d = 2, a + 4d = -4. Subtracting: 3d = -6, d = -2, a = 4. The 12th reciprocal is 4 + 11(-2) = -18, so the 12th H.P. term is -1/18.

lessons.title: Unit 4 Overview — Miscellaneous Series
lessons.notes_html:
This unit sums series that are neither pure A.P. nor pure G.P. The first tool is the sigma method: if the k-th term is a polynomial in k, split it into powers of k and use the three standard sums of k, k^2 and k^3.

The second tool handles an arithmetico-geometric (A.G.) series — an A.P. multiplied term-by-term by a G.P. — by the shift-and-subtract trick: write S, write rS underneath shifted by one place, and subtract.

Formula: Sum of k from 1 to n = n (n + 1) / 2

Formula: Sum of k^2 = n (n + 1) (2n + 1) / 6

Formula: Sum of k^3 = [n (n + 1) / 2]^2

Formula: A.G. series (a, d, r), infinite sum for |r| < 1: S_inf = a / (1 - r) + dr / (1 - r)^2

Formula: 1 / [k (k + 1)] = 1 / k - 1 / (k + 1) — such series telescope

Key Points

  • Always write the general (k-th) term first; the sum is then a combination of the three standard sums.
  • Check every sigma answer at n = 1 (and n = 2) before trusting it.
  • For an A.G. series, multiply by r and subtract — the A.P. part collapses to a G.P.
  • An infinite A.G. sum exists only when |r| < 1.
  • Word problems: decide first whether the pattern is an A.P. or a G.P., then use that unit’s formulas.

mcqs.q: What is the formula for the sum of the first n natural numbers, 1 + 2 + ... + n?
mcqs.why: The notes give sum of k from 1 to n = n(n + 1)/2. Check n = 2: 2 x 3/2 = 3 = 1 + 2, which is correct.

mcqs.q: What is the formula for 1^2 + 2^2 + ... + n^2?
mcqs.why: The notes give sum of k^2 = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6. Check n = 1: 1 x 2 x 3/6 = 1 = 1^2, which is correct.

mcqs.q: What is the formula for 1^3 + 2^3 + ... + n^3?
mcqs.why: The notes give sum of k^3 = [n(n + 1)/2]^2, the square of the sum of the first n numbers. Check n = 2: [2 x 3/2]^2 = 9 = 1 + 8.

mcqs.q: Using sum k = n(n + 1)/2, what is 1 + 2 + ... + 10?
mcqs.why: Substitute n = 10 in n(n + 1)/2: 10 x 11/2 = 110/2 = 55. Direct addition 1 + 2 + ... + 10 also gives 55.
Substitute n = 4: 4 x 5 x 9/6 = 180/6 = 30. Directly: 1 + 4 + 9 + 16 = 30, confirming the formula value.
Substitute n = 3: [3 x 4/2]^2 = 6^2 = 36. Directly: 1 + 8 + 27 = 36, confirming the formula value.

mcqs.q: An arithmetico-geometric (A.G.) series is formed by doing what?
options: Adding corresponding terms of an A.P. and a G.P. term by term
Multiplying all the terms of an A.P. together
Multiplying corresponding terms of an A.P. and a G.P. term by term
Adding all the terms of a G.P. together
mcqs.why: The overview defines an A.G. series as an A.P. multiplied term-by-term by a G.P., and it is summed by the shift-and-subtract trick.

mcqs.q: For an A.G. series with first A.P. term a, difference d and ratio r, what is the infinite sum S_inf?
mcqs.why: The notes give S_inf = a/(1 - r) + dr/(1 - r)^2. It comes from writing S, writing rS shifted by one place, and subtracting so the A.P. part collapses to a G.P.

mcqs.q: For which values of r does an infinite A.G. sum exist?
mcqs.why: The overview states that an infinite A.G. sum exists only when |r| < 1, because otherwise the terms do not shrink towards zero and the series diverges.

mcqs.q: The fraction 1/[k(k + 1)] splits into partial fractions as what?
mcqs.why: The notes give 1/[k(k + 1)] = 1/k - 1/(k + 1). Check: 1/k - 1/(k + 1) = [(k + 1) - k]/[k(k + 1)] = 1/[k(k + 1)], and such series telescope.

lessons.title: Exercise 4.1 (p.132) - Summing Series by the Sigma Method
lessons.notes_html:
Each series has a k-th term that is a product or a power pattern. Write T_k as a polynomial in k, split the sum into sums of k, k^2 and k^3, and use the three standard formulas.

Method note: Method used below: write the k-th term as a polynomial in k, then use sum k = n(n+1)/2, sum k^2 = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6, sum k^3 = [n(n+1)/2]^2. Each answer is checked for n = 1 (and n = 2 where shown).

In this exercise: 1. 1 x 3 + 2 x 6 + 3 x 9 + ... (up to n terms). 2. 5 x 5 + 7 x 9 + 9 x 13 + ... (up to n terms). 3. 1 x 5 + 2 x 8 + 3 x 11 + ... (up to n terms). 4. 3 x 4 x 7 + 4 x 6 x 10 + 5 x 8 x 13 + ... (up to n terms). 5. 1 x 4 x 6 + 4 x 7 x 10 + 7 x 10 x 14 + ... (up to n terms). 6. 1^2 + 4^2 + 7^2 + ... (up to n terms). 7. 3^2 + 6^2 + 9^2 + ... (up to n terms). 8. 1^3 + 4^3 + 7^3 + ... (up to n terms). 9. 3 x 1^2 + 5 x 2^2 + 7 x 3^2 + ... (up to n terms). 10. 5 x 2^2 + 7 x 3^2 + 9 x 4^2 + ... (up to n terms). 11. 1 + (1 + 2) + (1 + 2 + 3) + ... (up to n terms). 12. 2 + (2 + 5) + (2 + 5 + 8) + ... (up to n terms).

Worked Example: 1. 1 x 3 + 2 x 6 + 3 x 9 + ... (up to n terms).

Formula used: Sum k = n (n + 1) / 2; Sum k^2 = n (n + 1) (2n + 1) / 6; Sum k^3 = [n (n + 1) / 2]^2.

Step 1: The k-th term is k x 3k = 3k^2.

Step 2: Sum = 3 x n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6 = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/2. Check n = 1: 1 x 2 x 3/2 = 3.

Answer: n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/2

Worked Example: 4. 3 x 4 x 7 + 4 x 6 x 10 + 5 x 8 x 13 + ... (up to n terms).

Formula used: Sum k = n (n + 1) / 2; Sum k^2 = n (n + 1) (2n + 1) / 6; Sum k^3 = [n (n + 1) / 2]^2.

Step 1: The k-th term is (k + 2)(2k + 2)(3k + 4) = 2(k + 1)(k + 2)(3k + 4) = 6k^3 + 26k^2 + 36k + 16.

Step 2: Sum = 6[n(n + 1)/2]^2 + 26 x n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6 + 36 x n(n + 1)/2 + 16n.

Step 3: = (3/2)n^2(n + 1)^2 + (13/3)n(n + 1)(2n + 1) + 18n(n + 1) + 16n. Check n = 1: 6 + 26 + 36 + 16 = 84 = 3 x 4 x 7.

Answer: (3/2)n^2(n + 1)^2 + (13/3)n(n + 1)(2n + 1) + 18n(n + 1) + 16n

Worked Example: 7. 3^2 + 6^2 + 9^2 + ... (up to n terms).

Formula used: Sum k = n (n + 1) / 2; Sum k^2 = n (n + 1) (2n + 1) / 6; Sum k^3 = [n (n + 1) / 2]^2.

Step 1: The k-th term is (3k)^2 = 9k^2.

Step 2: Sum = 9 x n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6 = (3/2)n(n + 1)(2n + 1). Check n = 1: (3/2)(2)(3) = 9.

Answer: (3/2)n(n + 1)(2n + 1)

Worked Example: 9. 3 x 1^2 + 5 x 2^2 + 7 x 3^2 + ... (up to n terms).

Formula used: Sum k = n (n + 1) / 2; Sum k^2 = n (n + 1) (2n + 1) / 6; Sum k^3 = [n (n + 1) / 2]^2.

Step 1: The k-th term is (2k + 1)k^2 = 2k^3 + k^2.

Step 2: Sum = 2[n(n + 1)/2]^2 + n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6 = n(n + 1)(3n^2 + 5n + 1)/6. Check n = 1: 1 x 2 x 9/6 = 3.

Answer: n(n + 1)(3n^2 + 5n + 1)/6

Worked Example: 12. 2 + (2 + 5) + (2 + 5 + 8) + ... (up to n terms).

Formula used: Sum k = n (n + 1) / 2; Sum k^2 = n (n + 1) (2n + 1) / 6; Sum k^3 = [n (n + 1) / 2]^2.

Step 1: The k-th bracket is the sum of the A.P. 2, 5, 8, ... to k terms: (k/2)[4 + 3(k - 1)] = k(3k + 1)/2.

Step 2: Sum = (1/2)[3 sum k^2 + sum k] = (1/2)[3 x n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6 + n(n + 1)/2] = n(n + 1)^2/2.

Step 3: Check n = 2: 2 x 9/2 = 9 = 2 + 7.

Answer: n(n + 1)^2/2

mcqs.q: For the series 1 x 3 + 2 x 6 + 3 x 9 + ..., what is the k-th term?
mcqs.why: The k-th term is k x 3k = 3k^2, as in the worked example. Check k = 2: 3 x 4 = 12 = 2 x 6, the second term of the series.

mcqs.q: What is the sum to n terms of 1 x 3 + 2 x 6 + 3 x 9 + ...?
What is the sum of the first 2 terms of 1 x 3 + 2 x 6 + 3 x 9 + ...?
mcqs.why: Directly: 1 x 3 + 2 x 6 = 3 + 12 = 15. Formula check: n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/2 with n = 2 gives 2 x 3 x 5/2 = 15.

mcqs.q: For the series 3^2 + 6^2 + 9^2 + ..., what is the k-th term?
mcqs.why: The k-th base is 3k, so the k-th term is (3k)^2 = 9k^2, as in the worked example. Check k = 2: 9 x 4 = 36 = 6^2.

mcqs.q: What is the sum to n terms of 3^2 + 6^2 + 9^2 + ...?
What is the sum of the first 2 terms of 3^2 + 6^2 + 9^2 + ...?
mcqs.why: Directly: 3^2 + 6^2 = 9 + 36 = 45. Formula check: (3/2)n(n + 1)(2n + 1) with n = 2 gives (3/2) x 2 x 3 x 5 = 45.

mcqs.q: For the series 3 x 1^2 + 5 x 2^2 + 7 x 3^2 + ..., what is the k-th term as a polynomial in k?
mcqs.why: The k-th term is (2k + 1)k^2 = 2k^3 + k^2, as in the worked example. Check k = 2: 16 + 4 = 20 = 5 x 2^2.

mcqs.q: What is the sum to n terms of 3 x 1^2 + 5 x 2^2 + 7 x 3^2 + ...?
In the series 2 + (2 + 5) + (2 + 5 + 8) + ..., what is the k-th bracket?
mcqs.why: The k-th bracket is the A.P. 2, 5, 8, ... summed to k terms: (k/2)[4 + 3(k - 1)] = k(3k + 1)/2. Check k = 2: 2 x 7/2 = 7 = 2 + 5.

mcqs.q: What is the sum to n terms of 2 + (2 + 5) + (2 + 5 + 8) + ...?

lessons.title: Exercise 4.2 (p.135) - Arithmetico-Geometric Series
lessons.notes_html:
Sum an A.G. series to n terms and to infinity. The method note at the head of the exercise gives the closed formulas; the worked examples show the shift-and-subtract working behind them.

Method note: Sum of n terms and infinite terms of the following. For an arithmetico-geometric series with first term a, difference d and ratio r: S_n = a/(1 - r) + dr/(1 - r)^2 - dr^n/(1 - r)^2 - [a + (n - 1)d]r^n/(1 - r); and S_inf = a/(1 - r) + dr/(1 - r)^2 when |r| < 1.

In this exercise: 1. 1 + 2.3 + 3.3^2 + 4.3^3 + ... (i.e. 1 + 2 x 3 + 3 x 3^2 + 4 x 3^3 + ...). Sum of n terms and infinite terms. 2. 1 + 6x + 11x^2 + 16x^3 + ... Sum of n terms and infinite terms. 3. 1 + 4/5 + 7/25 + 10/125 + ... Sum of n terms and infinite terms. 4. 1 + 7/4 + 13/4^2 + 19/4^3 + ... Sum of n terms and infinite terms. 5. 1 - 6y + 11y^2 - 16y^3 + ... Sum of n terms and infinite terms. 6. Find S_8 if 1 + 5/2 + 9/4 + 13/8 +. 7. Find n-th term if 3, 7/3, 11/3^2, 15/3^3. 8. Find 15th term if 9, 14/5, 19/5^2.

Worked Example: 1. 1 + 2.3 + 3.3^2 + 4.3^3 + ... (i.e. 1 + 2 x 3 + 3 x 3^2 + 4 x 3^3 + ...). Sum of n terms and infinite terms.

Formula used: S_n = a / (1 - r) + dr / (1 - r)^2 - dr^n / (1 - r)^2 - [a + (n - 1) d] r^n / (1 - r); S_inf = a / (1 - r) + dr / (1 - r)^2 for |r| < 1.

Step 1: Here a = 1, d = 1, r = 3.

Step 2: S_n = 1/(1 - 3) + 3/(1 - 3)^2 - 3^n/(1 - 3)^2 - n x 3^n/(1 - 3) = -1/2 + 3/4 - 3^n/4 + n x 3^n/2 = [1 + (2n - 1)3^n]/4.

Step 3: Check n = 1: [1 + 3]/4 = 1; n = 2: [1 + 27]/4 = 7 = 1 + 6.

Step 4: Since |r| = 3 >= 1, the infinite sum does not exist (the series diverges).

Answer: S_n = [1 + (2n - 1)3^n]/4; the infinite sum diverges (r = 3)

Worked Example: 3. 1 + 4/5 + 7/25 + 10/125 + ... Sum of n terms and infinite terms.

Formula used: S_n = a / (1 - r) + dr / (1 - r)^2 - dr^n / (1 - r)^2 - [a + (n - 1) d] r^n / (1 - r); S_inf = a / (1 - r) + dr / (1 - r)^2 for |r| < 1.

Step 1: Here a = 1, d = 3, r = 1/5.

Step 2: S_inf = 1/(1 - 1/5) + 3(1/5)/(1 - 1/5)^2 = 5/4 + 15/16 = 35/16.

Step 3: S_n = 35/16 - (1/5)^n[3/(1 - 1/5)^2 + (3n - 2)/(1 - 1/5)] = 35/16 - (1/5)^n(60n + 35)/16 = [35 - (60n + 35)/5^n]/16.

Step 4: Check n = 1: [35 - 95/5]/16 = 16/16 = 1.

Answer: S_n = [35 - (60n + 35)/5^n]/16; S_inf = 35/16

Worked Example: 5. 1 - 6y + 11y^2 - 16y^3 + ... Sum of n terms and infinite terms.

Formula used: S_n = a / (1 - r) + dr / (1 - r)^2 - dr^n / (1 - r)^2 - [a + (n - 1) d] r^n / (1 - r); S_inf = a / (1 - r) + dr / (1 - r)^2 for |r| < 1.

Step 1: Write the terms as (a + kd)r^k with r = -y: the first term gives a = 1; the second gives (a + d)(-y) = -6y, so d = 5 (check: third term (1 + 10)y^2 = 11y^2; fourth (1 + 15)(-y)^3 = -16y^3).

Step 2: So a = 1, d = 5, r = -y. Then S_n = 1/(1 + y) + 5(-y)/(1 + y)^2 - 5(-y)^n/(1 + y)^2 - [1 + 5(n - 1)](-y)^n/(1 + y).

Step 3: For |y| < 1, S_inf = 1/(1 + y) - 5y/(1 + y)^2 = (1 - 4y)/(1 + y)^2.

Answer: S_n = 1/(1 + y) - 5y/(1 + y)^2 - 5(-y)^n/(1 + y)^2 - [1 + 5(n - 1)](-y)^n/(1 + y); S_inf = (1 - 4y)/(1 + y)^2 for |y| < 1

Worked Example: 6. Find S_8 if 1 + 5/2 + 9/4 + 13/8 + ...

Formula used: S_n = a / (1 - r) + dr / (1 - r)^2 - dr^n / (1 - r)^2 - [a + (n - 1) d] r^n / (1 - r); S_inf = a / (1 - r) + dr / (1 - r)^2 for |r| < 1.

Step 1: Here a = 1, d = 4, r = 1/2.

Step 2: S_n = 1/(1 - 1/2) + 4(1/2)/(1 - 1/2)^2 - (1/2)^n[4/(1 - 1/2)^2 + (4n - 3)/(1 - 1/2)] = 10 - (8n + 10)/2^n.

Step 3: Check n = 1: 10 - 18/2 = 1.

Step 4: Hence S_8 = 10 - 74/256 = 10 - 37/128 = 1243/128.

Answer: S_8 = 1243/128

Worked Example: 8. Find 15th term if 9, 14/5, 19/5^2, ...

Formula used: S_n = a / (1 - r) + dr / (1 - r)^2 - dr^n / (1 - r)^2 - [a + (n - 1) d] r^n / (1 - r); S_inf = a / (1 - r) + dr / (1 - r)^2 for |r| < 1.

Step 1: This is arithmetico-geometric with a = 9, d = 5, r = 1/5.

Step 2: The 15th term is (9 + 14 x 5)(1/5)^{14} = 79/5^{14}.

Answer: 79/5^14

mcqs.q: For the A.G. series 1 + 2 x 3 + 3 x 3^2 + 4 x 3^3 + ..., what are a, d and r?
mcqs.why: The A.P. part is 1, 2, 3, 4, ... so a = 1 and d = 1; the G.P. part is 1, 3, 3^2, ... so r = 3, exactly as stated in the worked example.

mcqs.q: What is the sum to n terms of 1 + 2 x 3 + 3 x 3^2 + 4 x 3^3 + ...?
Does the series 1 + 2 x 3 + 3 x 3^2 + 4 x 3^3 + ... have an infinite sum?
mcqs.why: An infinite A.G. sum needs |r| < 1. Here |r| = 3 which is not less than 1, so the infinite sum does not exist and the series diverges, as the worked example states.

mcqs.q: For the A.G. series 1 + 4/5 + 7/25 + 10/125 + ..., what are a, d and r?
mcqs.why: The A.P. part is 1, 4, 7, 10, ... so a = 1 and d = 3; the G.P. part is 1, 1/5, 1/25, ... so r = 1/5, exactly as stated in the worked example.

mcqs.q: What is the infinite sum of 1 + 4/5 + 7/25 + 10/125 + ...?
What is the sum to n terms of 1 + 4/5 + 7/25 + 10/125 + ...?
For the series 1 + 5/2 + 9/4 + 13/8 + ..., the sum to n terms is S_n = 10 - (8n + 10)/2^n. What is S_8?
What is the 15th term of the A.G. series 9, 14/5, 19/5^2, ...?
For the series 1 - 6y + 11y^2 - 16y^3 + ..., written with r = -y, what is the infinite sum for |y| < 1?
What is the n-th term of the A.G. series 3, 7/3, 11/3^2, 15/3^3, ...?
mcqs.why: The A.P. part is 3, 7, 11, 15, ... with a = 3, d = 4, so its n-th term is 3 + 4(n - 1) = 4n - 1; the G.P. part gives r^(n - 1) = (1/3)^(n - 1). So T_n = (4n - 1)/3^(n - 1). Check n = 2: 7/3, correct.

lessons.title: Exercise 4.3 (p.143) - Word Problems on A.P. and G.P.
lessons.notes_html:
Real-life problems — savings, instalments, falling bodies, bacteria growth — that become an A.P. or a G.P. once the pattern is spotted. Take three numbers in A.P. as a - d, a, a + d and in G.P. as a/r, a, ar when a sum and a product are both given.

In this exercise: 1. A man deposits in a bank Rs 15,000 in the first month; Rs 16,500 in the second month; Rs 18,000 in third month and so on. Find how much he will have deposited in the bank in 12th month. 2. A boy saves Rs 100 at the end of first week and goes on increasing his saving Rs 15 weekly. After some weeks, he saves Rs 1000. In how many weeks he will save Rs 1000. 3. An object falling from rest, falls 16 meter during the first second, 32 meter during the next second, 48 meters during the third second and so on. How far will it fall during the 9th second. 4. The sum of three numbers in A.P. is 21 and their product is 231. Find the numbers. 5. Find five numbers in A.P. whose sum is 20 and the sum of whose cubes is 440. 6. The sum of Rs 21,000 is distributed among five persons so that each person after the first receives Rs 40 less than the preceding person. How much does each person receive. 7. Tickets for a certain show were printed bearing numbers from 1 to 150. Odd number tickets were sold by receiving rupees equal to twice of the number on the ticket while even number tickets were. 8. A man borrows Rs 1,450 and agree to repay with a total interest of Rs 350 in 15 installments, each installment being less than the preceding by Rs 20. What should be his first installment. 9. Find three consecutive numbers in G.P. whose sum is 21 and their product is 216. 10. The number of bacteria in a culture increased geometrically from 625,000 to 18,75,000 in 7 days. Find the daily rate of increase assuming the rate to be constant.

Worked Example: 1. A man deposits in a bank Rs 15,000 in the first month; Rs 16,500 in the second month; Rs 18,000 in third month and so on. Find how much he will have deposited in the bank in 12th month.

Formula used: A.P.: a_n = a1 + (n - 1) d, S_n = (n/2) (a1 + a_n); G.P.: a_n = a1 r^(n - 1), S_n = a1 (r^n - 1) / (r - 1).

Step 1: The monthly deposits form an A.P.: 15000, 16500, 18000, ... with first term 15000 and common difference 1500.

Step 2: Deposit in the 12th month = 15000 + 11(1500) = 15000 + 16500 = 31500.

Step 3: (For reference, the total deposited over 12 months is (12/2)[2(15000) + 11(1500)] = 6(46500) = 279000.)

Answer: Rs 31,500 deposited in the 12th month (Rs 279,000 deposited in total over 12 months)

Worked Example: 3. An object falling from rest, falls 16 meter during the first second, 32 meter during the next second, 48 meters during the third second and so on. How far will it fall during the 9th second?

Formula used: A.P.: a_n = a1 + (n - 1) d, S_n = (n/2) (a1 + a_n); G.P.: a_n = a1 r^(n - 1), S_n = a1 (r^n - 1) / (r - 1).

Step 1: The distances per second form an A.P.: 16, 32, 48, ... with first term 16 and common difference 16.

Step 2: Distance during the 9th second = 16 + 8(16) = 16(9) = 144 metres.

Answer: 144 metres

Worked Example: 5. Find five numbers in A.P. whose sum is 20 and the sum of whose cubes is 440.

Formula used: A.P.: a_n = a1 + (n - 1) d, S_n = (n/2) (a1 + a_n); G.P.: a_n = a1 r^(n - 1), S_n = a1 (r^n - 1) / (r - 1).

Step 1: Let the numbers be a - 2d, a - d, a, a + d, a + 2d. Their sum is 5a = 20, so a = 4.

Step 2: Sum of cubes = (a - 2d)^3 + (a - d)^3 + a^3 + (a + d)^3 + (a + 2d)^3 = 5a^3 + 30a d^2.

Step 3: With a = 4: 320 + 120 d^2 = 440, so d^2 = 1 and d = +-1.

Step 4: The numbers are 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.

Answer: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6

Worked Example: 8. A man borrows Rs 1,450 and agree to repay with a total interest of Rs 350 in 15 installments, each installment being less than the preceding by Rs 20. What should be his first installment?

Formula used: A.P.: a_n = a1 + (n - 1) d, S_n = (n/2) (a1 + a_n); G.P.: a_n = a1 r^(n - 1), S_n = a1 (r^n - 1) / (r - 1).

Step 1: Total to repay = 1450 + 350 = 1800, in 15 installments forming an A.P. with common difference -20.

Step 2: Sum = (15/2)[2a + 14(-20)] = 15(a - 140) = 1800, so a - 140 = 120 and a = 260.

Step 3: The first installment is Rs 260. Flag: with a = 260 and d = -20, the 15th installment would be 260 - 280 = -20, i.e. negative — the book's numbers (15 installments, Rs 20 steps, Rs 1800 total) cannot all hold for real installments; the answer follows the book's data as printed.

Answer: Rs 260 (flag: the book's data are inconsistent — see steps)

Worked Example: 10. The number of bacteria in a culture increased geometrically from 625,000 to 18,75,000 in 7 days. Find the daily rate of increase assuming the rate to be constant.

Formula used: A.P.: a_n = a1 + (n - 1) d, S_n = (n/2) (a1 + a_n); G.P.: a_n = a1 r^(n - 1), S_n = a1 (r^n - 1) / (r - 1).

Step 1: Let the daily growth factor be r. Over 7 days the number is multiplied by r^7: 625000 x r^7 = 1875000.

Step 2: So r^7 = 3, giving r = 3^{1/7} = 1.1699... to four places.

Step 3: The daily rate of increase is r - 1 = 0.1699..., i.e. about 17% per day.

Answer: Daily growth factor 3^{1/7}, i.e. a daily rate of about 17%

mcqs.q: A man deposits Rs 15,000 in the first month, Rs 16,500 in the second, Rs 18,000 in the third, and so on. How much does he deposit in the 12th month?
With deposits of Rs 15,000, Rs 16,500, Rs 18,000, ... each month, what is the total deposited over 12 months?
An object falls 16 m in the first second, 32 m in the next, 48 m in the third, and so on. How far does it fall during the 9th second?
mcqs.why: The distances form an A.P. with a1 = 16 and d = 16. a_9 = 16 + (9 - 1) x 16 = 16 + 128 = 144, i.e. 144 metres during the 9th second.

mcqs.q: Three numbers in A.P. have sum 21 and product 231. What are the numbers?
mcqs.why: Take the numbers as a - d, a, a + d. Sum: 3a = 21 so a = 7. Product: a(a^2 - d^2) = 231 gives 7(49 - d^2) = 231, so 49 - d^2 = 33, d^2 = 16, d = 4. Numbers: 3, 7, 11.

mcqs.q: Five numbers in A.P. have sum 20 and the sum of their cubes is 440. What are the numbers?
mcqs.why: Take a - 2d, a - d, a, a + d, a + 2d. Sum 5a = 20 gives a = 4. Sum of cubes = 5a^3 + 30a d^2 = 320 + 120 d^2 = 440, so d^2 = 1. The numbers are 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.

mcqs.q: In the five-number A.P. problem (sum 20, sum of cubes 440), what is the middle number a?
mcqs.why: Taking the five numbers as a - 2d, a - d, a, a + d, a + 2d, their sum is 5a. Setting 5a = 20 gives a = 20/5 = 4, the middle number of the A.P.

mcqs.q: Rs 21,000 is shared among five persons, each after the first getting Rs 40 less than the one before. How much does the first person get?
mcqs.why: The shares form an A.P.: a, a - 40, a - 80, a - 120, a - 160. Sum = 5a - 400 = 21000, so 5a = 21400 and a = 4280. The first person gets Rs 4,280.

mcqs.q: A man repays Rs 1,450 plus Rs 350 interest in 15 instalments, each Rs 20 less than the previous one. What is his first instalment (following the book's data)?
mcqs.why: Total to repay = 1450 + 350 = 1800. Sum = (15/2)[2a + 14(-20)] = 15(a - 140) = 1800, so a - 140 = 120 and a = 260. First instalment Rs 260, following the book's data as printed.

mcqs.q: Three consecutive numbers in G.P. have sum 21 and product 216. What are the numbers?
mcqs.why: Take the numbers as a/r, a, ar. Product a^3 = 216 gives a = 6. Sum: 6(1/r + 1 + r) = 21 gives r + 1/r = 5/2, so 2r^2 - 5r + 2 = 0 and r = 2 (or 1/2). The numbers are 3, 6, 12.

mcqs.q: Bacteria grow geometrically from 625,000 to 1,875,000 in 7 days. What is the approximate daily rate of increase?

lessons.title: Review Exercise 4 (pp.144-145)
lessons.notes_html:
Review of Unit 4: sigma sums, arithmetico-geometric series (finite and infinite), and telescoping terms.

In this exercise: 1. Choose the correct options. 2. Sum the series up to n terms.

Worked Example: 1(i). A series which is obtained by multiplying corresponding terms of arithmetic and geometric series is known as;

a) arithmetic series   b) geometric series   c) arithmetic-geometric series   d) harmonic series

Answer: c) arithmetic-geometric series

Worked Example: 1(ii). n-th term of arithmetic-geometric series is;

a) a_1 + (n - 1)d   b) a_1 r^{n-1}   c) [a_1 + (n - 1)d] r^{n-1}   d) 1/(a_1 + (n - 1)d)

Answer: c) [a_1 + (n - 1)d] r^{n-1}

Worked Example: 1(iii). Sum_{k=1}^{4} (k^2 + k) is equal to;

a) 36   b) 40   c) 44   d) 48

Answer: b) 40

Worked Example: 1(iv). Sum of infinite arithmetic geometric series is obtained by the formula.

a) a/(1 - r)   b) dr/(1 - r)^2   c) a/(1 - r) + dr/(1 - r)^2   d) a/(1 - r) + dr/(1 - r)^3

Answer: c) a/(1 - r) + dr/(1 - r)^2

Worked Example: 1(v). Sum_{x=1}^{4} x^2 =

a) 25   b) 30   c) 35   d) 40

Answer: b) 30

Worked Example: 1(vi). Sum_{k=1}^{n} k^2 =

a) n   b) n(n + 1)/2   c) n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6   d) [n(n + 1)/2]^2

Answer: c) n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6

Worked Example: 1(vii). Sum of infinite term of arithmetic geometric series is

a) a/(1 - r)   b) dr/(1 - r)^2   c) a/(1 - r) + dr/(1 - r)^2   d) a/(1 - r) + dr/(1 - r)^2 + dr^n/(1 - r)^2

Answer: c) a/(1 - r) + dr/(1 - r)^2

Worked Example: 1(viii). S_inf = a/(1 - r) +

a) dr/(1 - r)^2   b) dr/(1 - r)^2   c) dr/(1 - r^2)   d) d^2 r/(1 + r^2)

Answer: b) dr/(1 - r)^2

Worked Example: 1(ix). 1/[n(n + 1)] =

a) 1/n + 1/(n + 1)   b) 1/n - 1/(n + 1)   c) 2/n + 1/(n + 1)   d) 1/n - 3/(n + 1)

Answer: b) 1/n - 1/(n + 1)

Worked Example: 2. Sum the series up to n terms. (i) 2 x 1^2 + 4 x 2^2 + 6 x 2^3 + ... (ii) 1 + 4/3 + 7/3^2 + ...

Formula used: See the formulas in the Unit 4 Overview and Lessons 1 to 3 of this unit.

Step 1: (i) Flag: as printed (verified at 300 dpi: 2 x 1^2 + 4 x 2^2 + 6 x 2^3 + ...), the terms 2, 16, 48, ... do not form a standard arithmetico-geometric series. The sum below follows the evident continuation 2 x 1^2 + 4 x 2^2 + 6 x 2^3 + 8 x 2^4 + ..., i.e. T_k = 2k x 2^k for k >= 2 with T_1 = 2.

Step 2: Sum = 2 + sum_{k=2}^{n} k x 2^{k+1} = 2 + 2[(n - 1)2^{n+1} + 2] - 4 = (n - 1)2^{n+2} + 2. Check n = 2: 2^4 + 2 = 18 = 2 + 16; n = 3: 2 x 2^5 + 2 = 66 = 2 + 16 + 48.

Step 3: (ii) Here a = 1, d = 3, r = 1/3. S_inf = 1/(2/3) + 3(1/3)/(4/9) = 15/4.

Step 4: S_n = 15/4 - (1/3)^n[3/(4/9) + (3n - 2)/(2/3)] = 15/4 - (1/3)^n(18n + 15)/4 = [15 - (18n + 15)/3^n]/4. Check n = 1: [15 - 33/3]/4 = 1.

Answer: (i) S_n = (n - 1)2^{n+2} + 2, for the series as printed (flagged — see steps); (ii) S_n = [15 - (18n + 15)/3^n]/4

mcqs.q: A series obtained by multiplying corresponding terms of an arithmetic series and a geometric series is known as what?
mcqs.why: This is Review Exercise 4, Q1(i): multiplying corresponding terms of an A.P. and a G.P. gives an arithmetic-geometric series, option (c) in the book.

mcqs.q: What is the n-th term of an arithmetic-geometric series?
mcqs.why: Review Q1(ii): the n-th A.P. factor is a1 + (n - 1)d and the n-th G.P. factor is r^(n - 1), so T_n = [a1 + (n - 1)d] r^(n - 1), option (c) in the book.

mcqs.q: What is the value of sum from k = 1 to 4 of (k^2 + k)?
mcqs.why: Sum k^2 for k = 1 to 4 = 4 x 5 x 9/6 = 30 and sum k = 4 x 5/2 = 10, so the total is 30 + 10 = 40. Directly: 2 + 6 + 12 + 20 = 40.

mcqs.q: The sum of an infinite arithmetic-geometric series is obtained by which formula?
mcqs.why: Review Q1(iv): S_inf = a/(1 - r) + dr/(1 - r)^2, option (c) in the book. Both parts are needed: the first from a and the second from d and r.

mcqs.q: What is the value of sum from x = 1 to 4 of x^2?
Sum from k = 1 to n of k^2 equals which expression?
mcqs.why: Review Q1(vi): sum of k^2 = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6, option (c) in the book. The option n(n + 1)/2 is the sum of k, and its square is the sum of k^3.

mcqs.q: 1/[n(n + 1)] is equal to which difference?
mcqs.why: Review Q1(ix): 1/n - 1/(n + 1) = [(n + 1) - n]/[n(n + 1)] = 1/[n(n + 1)], option (b) in the book. This split makes the series telescope.

mcqs.q: What is the infinite sum of the A.G. series 1 + 4/3 + 7/3^2 + ...?
What is the sum to n terms of 1 + 4/3 + 7/3^2 + ...?
For the series as printed in Review Q2(i), 2 x 1^2 + 4 x 2^2 + 6 x 2^3 + ..., the notes give the sum to n terms as what?
mcqs.why: The notes flag this series as printed and sum the evident continuation T_k = 2k x 2^k (k at least 2) with T_1 = 2, giving S_n = (n - 1)2^(n + 2) + 2. Check n = 2: 2^4 + 2 = 18 = 2 + 16.

chapters.title: Unit 5: Permutation and Combination and Probability

lessons.title: Unit 5 Overview — Permutation and Combination and Probability
lessons.notes_html:
Counting starts with the multiplication principle: if one task can be done in m ways and the next in n ways, both together can be done in m x n ways. Arranging r objects chosen from n, where order matters, gives a permutation nPr; choosing them where order does not matter gives a combination nCr.

Probability measures chance on the same counting base: for equally likely outcomes, P(E) = (number of favourable outcomes) / (total number of outcomes).

Formula: n! = n (n - 1) (n - 2) ... 2 x 1, and 0! = 1

Formula: nPr = n! / (n - r)!; arrangements of n different objects = n!

Formula: nCr = n! / (r! (n - r)!); nCr = nC(n - r); nCr + nC(r - 1) = (n + 1)Cr

Formula: Repeated letters: arrangements = n! / (p! q! ...) for p, q, ... alike

Formula: Circular arrangements of n objects = (n - 1)!; on a key ring (flips the same) = (n - 1)! / 2

Formula: P(E) = n(E) / n(S); P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B); P(not E) = 1 - P(E)

Key Points

  • Order matters → permutation; order does not matter → combination.
  • For arrangements with some letters alike, divide by the factorial of each repeat count.
  • Committees and selections are combinations — split into cases (exactly / at most / at least) and add.
  • With replacement, the sample space stays the same size at each draw; without replacement it shrinks.
  • Diagonals of an n-sided figure = nC2 - n (all joins minus the sides).

mcqs.q: If one task can be done in m ways and a second task in n ways, in how many ways can both be done together?
mcqs.why: This is the multiplication principle in the overview: each of the m ways for the first task can pair with each of the n ways for the second, giving m x n ways in total.

mcqs.q: What is the value of 0!?
mcqs.why: The overview states the definition n! = n(n - 1)(n - 2)...2 x 1 together with the special value 0! = 1, which is needed for formulas like nCr to work at the ends.

mcqs.q: Which formula gives the number of permutations nPr (arrangements of r objects chosen from n)?
mcqs.why: The overview gives nPr = n!/(n - r)!. Order matters in a permutation, so arranging r from n fills r ordered places: n(n - 1)...(n - r + 1) = n!/(n - r)!.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly matches counting type to whether order matters?
options: Order matters: combination; order does not matter: permutation
Order matters: permutation; order does not matter: combination
Order matters in both permutation and combination
Order matters in neither permutation nor combination
mcqs.why: The Key Points state it directly: order matters means permutation (nPr); order does not matter means combination (nCr). Committees and selections are combinations.

mcqs.q: nCr is equal to which other combination (the symmetry property)?
mcqs.why: The overview gives nCr = nC(n - r), because n!/(r!(n - r)!) is unchanged when r and n - r are swapped: choosing r to take is the same as choosing n - r to leave.

mcqs.q: If n different letters include p alike of one kind and q alike of another, the number of arrangements is what?
mcqs.why: The overview gives arrangements = n!/(p! q! ...) for repeated letters: start with n! and divide by the factorial of each repeat count, since swapping alike letters changes nothing.

mcqs.q: In how many ways can n different objects be arranged around a circle?
mcqs.why: The overview gives circular arrangements of n objects = (n - 1)!: rotations of the whole circle are the same arrangement, which removes a factor of n from n!.

mcqs.q: In how many ways can n objects be arranged on a key ring, where flipping the ring gives the same arrangement?
mcqs.why: The overview gives key-ring arrangements = (n - 1)!/2: take the circular count (n - 1)! and divide by 2 because the ring can be flipped over without making a new arrangement.

mcqs.q: If P(E) is the probability of an event E, what is P(not E)?
mcqs.why: The overview gives P(not E) = 1 - P(E), since E either happens or does not happen, so P(E) + P(not E) = 1 and therefore P(not E) = 1 - P(E).

mcqs.q: How many diagonals does an n-sided plane figure have?
mcqs.why: The Key Points give diagonals = nC2 - n: joining every pair of vertices gives nC2 segments, and n of those joins are the sides of the figure, not diagonals.

lessons.title: Exercise 5.1 (p.154) - Permutations and Factorials
lessons.notes_html:
Counting arrangements: factorials simplified, words formed from letters (with repeats handled by dividing), books kept together on a shelf, signals from flags, numbers formed from digits, and arrangements around a round table and on a key ring.

In this exercise: 1. A student must choose 1 subject from each of 4 categories: Maths (4 options), Science (3 options), Humanities (2 options) and Art (5 options). How many different schedules are possible. 2. P, Q and R are the vertices of a triangle. In how many ways, can we write the triangles. 3. Evaluate the following. 4. Express the following in a single fraction. 5. In how many ways different batting orders are possible for a cricket team consisting of 11 players. 6. In how many ways can five English books, two chemistry books and four mathematics books arranged on a shelf so that all books of same kind are together. 7. How many different arrangement can be formed of the word 'NOSHKI' using all letters when no letter is to be repeated. 8. How many signals can be given by 7 flags of different colours when any number of them are used at a time. 9. Find the value of n in each of the following. 10. How many 5-digit numbers can be formed, without repeating any digit from the digits 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8. 11. How many words can be formed out of the letters of the following words, all letters taken together. 12. How many 8 digit numbers can be formed from the digits 1, 1, 1, 3, 3, 3, 5, 6? How many among these are greater than 50000000. 13. How many distinct permutations of letters of the word 'ESSENTIAL' are possible? How many will have the two S's. 14. 14 members of a club form 3 committees of 6, 5, 3 members so that no member is a member of more than one committee. Find the number of committees. 15. In how many ways can 7 persons be seated at a round table. 16. In how many ways 6 keys be arranged on a circular key ring.

Worked Example: 1. A student must choose 1 subject from each of 4 categories: Maths (4 options), Science (3 options), Humanities (2 options) and Art (5 options). How many different schedules are possible?

Formula used: nPr = n! / (n - r)!; all letters used with repeats p, q, ...: n! / (p! q! ...); round table (n - 1)!; key ring (n - 1)! / 2.

Step 1: By the fundamental counting principle, multiply the numbers of options: 4 x 3 x 2 x 5 = 120.

Answer: 120 schedules

Worked Example: 4. Express the following in a single fraction. (i) (n - 1)!/r! + (n + 1)!/(r - 1)!; (ii) n!/r! + (n - 1)!/(r + 1)! - (n - 2)!/(r - 1)!

Formula used: nPr = n! / (n - r)!; all letters used with repeats p, q, ...: n! / (p! q! ...); round table (n - 1)!; key ring (n - 1)! / 2.

Step 1: (i) Write the second term over r!: (n + 1)!/(r - 1)! = r(n + 1)!/r!. Sum = [(n - 1)! + r(n + 1)!]/r!. Since (n + 1)! = (n + 1)n(n - 1)!, this is (n - 1)![1 + r n(n + 1)]/r!.

Step 2: (ii) Use the common denominator (r + 1)!: n!/r! = n!(r + 1)/(r + 1)! and (n - 2)!/(r - 1)! = (n - 2)!r(r + 1)/(r + 1)!. Sum = [n!(r + 1) + (n - 1)! - (n - 2)!r(r + 1)]/(r + 1)! = (n - 2)![n(n - 1)(r + 1) + (n - 1) - r(r + 1)]/(r + 1)!.

Answer: (i) (n - 1)![1 + r n(n + 1)]/r!; (ii) (n - 2)![n(n - 1)(r + 1) + (n - 1) - r(r + 1)]/(r + 1)!

Worked Example: 7. How many different arrangement can be formed of the word 'NOSHKI' using all letters when no letter is to be repeated?

Formula used: nPr = n! / (n - r)!; all letters used with repeats p, q, ...: n! / (p! q! ...); round table (n - 1)!; key ring (n - 1)! / 2.

Step 1: NOSHKI has 6 distinct letters. Arrangements = 6! = 720.

Answer: 720

Worked Example: 10. How many 5-digit numbers can be formed, without repeating any digit from the digits 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8?

Formula used: nPr = n! / (n - r)!; all letters used with repeats p, q, ...: n! / (p! q! ...); round table (n - 1)!; key ring (n - 1)! / 2.

Step 1: Choose and arrange 5 out of 6 distinct digits: P(6, 5) = 6 x 5 x 4 x 3 x 2 = 720.

Answer: 720

Worked Example: 13. How many distinct permutations of letters of the word 'ESSENTIAL' are possible? How many will have the two S's (i) together (ii) separate. (Flag: ESSENTIAL has three S's; 'two S's' is read as the S's as a group — all three together, no two adjacent, and exactly two together are all given.)

Formula used: nPr = n! / (n - r)!; all letters used with repeats p, q, ...: n! / (p! q! ...); round table (n - 1)!; key ring (n - 1)! / 2.

Step 1: ESSENTIAL: 9 letters with E x 2, S x 3. Total = 9!/(2! x 3!) = 362880/12 = 30,240.

Step 2: (i) All three S's together: treat SSS as one block; 7 objects with E x 2 give 7!/2! = 2,520.

Step 3: (ii) No two S's adjacent: arrange the other 6 letters (E x 2, N, T, I, A, L) in 6!/2! = 360 ways; the 3 S's go into 3 of the 7 gaps: C(7, 3) = 35. Count = 360 x 35 = 12,600.

Step 4: Exactly two S's together (for completeness) = 30240 - 2520 - 12600 = 15,120.

Answer: 30,240 in total; all three S's together: 2,520; no two S's together: 12,600; exactly two S's together: 15,120

Worked Example: 16. In how many ways 6 keys be arranged on a circular key ring?

Formula used: nPr = n! / (n - r)!; all letters used with repeats p, q, ...: n! / (p! q! ...); round table (n - 1)!; key ring (n - 1)! / 2.

Step 1: On a key ring, arrangements that differ only by flipping the ring over are the same, so divide the circular count by 2: (6 - 1)!/2 = 120/2 = 60. (If flipping were not identified, the count would be (6 - 1)! = 120.)

Answer: 60 (flag: key-ring convention — see steps)

mcqs.q: A student chooses 1 subject from each of 4 categories: Maths (4 options), Science (3), Humanities (2) and Art (5). How many different schedules are possible?
mcqs.why: By the fundamental counting principle, multiply the options: 4 x 3 x 2 x 5 = 120. So there are 120 different schedules, as in the worked example.

mcqs.q: In how many different batting orders can a cricket team of 11 players be arranged?
mcqs.why: All 11 players are arranged in order, giving 11! = 11 x 10 x ... x 1 = 39916800. So there are 39,916,800 possible batting orders.

mcqs.q: How many different arrangements can be formed of the word NOSHKI, using all its letters with no repeat?
mcqs.why: NOSHKI has 6 distinct letters, so the arrangements are 6! = 6 x 5 x 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 = 720, exactly as in the worked example.

mcqs.q: How many 5-digit numbers can be formed without repeating a digit, from the digits 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8?
mcqs.why: Choose and arrange 5 out of 6 distinct digits: P(6, 5) = 6!/(6 - 5)! = 6 x 5 x 4 x 3 x 2 = 720, exactly as in the worked example.

mcqs.q: Five English books, two chemistry books and four mathematics books are arranged on a shelf so that all books of the same kind stay together. In how many ways?
