mcqs.why: tan(30 degrees) = vertical speed / horizontal speed, so horizontal speed = 500 / tan(30 degrees) = 500 / (1/sqrt(3)) = 500 sqrt(3) m/min, which is about 866 m/min.

mcqs.q: Express sin(3x) as a sum of trigonometric functions by writing 3x = 2x + x.
mcqs.why: Use sin(A + B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B with A = 2x, B = x: sin(3x) = sin(2x + x) = sin(2x)cos(x) + cos(2x)sin(x), which simplifies to 3 sin(x) - 4 sin^3(x).

mcqs.q: Which expression equals sin(3x)?
mcqs.why: Expanding sin(3x) = sin(2x)cos(x) + cos(2x)sin(x) and simplifying with the double-angle formulas gives the triple-angle result sin(3x) = 3 sin(x) - 4 sin^3(x), as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: Determine whether g(x) = cos(2x) is even, odd, or neither.
mcqs.why: Test with -x: g(-x) = cos(-2x) = cos(2x) = g(x), because cosine is even. Since g(-x) = g(x), g is an even function.

mcqs.q: Find the period of h(x) = tan(4x).
mcqs.why: Period of tan(bx) = pi / |b|. Substituting b = 4 gives period = pi / 4, so tan(4x) repeats every pi/4.

mcqs.q: Given P(x) = 3 - 4 sin(x), find its maximum value.
mcqs.why: sin(x) ranges over [-1, 1]. P is largest when sin(x) = -1: maximum = 3 - 4(-1) = 3 + 4 = 7. (The minimum, at sin(x) = 1, is 3 - 4 = -1.)

lessons.title: Review Exercise 10 (pp.322-323)
lessons.notes_html:
Review of Unit 10: ranges, periods, even and odd functions, extreme values and one sketch.

In this exercise: 1. Choose the correct options. 2. Find the maximum and minimum value of the each of the following functions. 3. Sketch the graph of y = 2sin(x), 0 <= x <= 2pi.

Worked Example: 1(i). The range of both the sine and cosine function is;

a) -inf < y < inf   b) -1 < y < 1   c) -1 <= y <= 1   d) 0 <= y <= 1

Answer: c) -1 <= y <= 1

Worked Example: 1(ii). If f(-x) = f(x), then the function is;

a) periodic   b) even   c) odd   d) rational

Answer: b) even

Worked Example: 1(iii). If f(x + p) = f(x) then the function is;

a) linear   b) quadratic   c) even   d) periodic

Answer: d) periodic

Worked Example: 1(iv). The period of tan(x) is;

a) pi/2   b) pi   c) 3pi/2   d) 2pi

Answer: b) pi

Worked Example: 1(v). The range of both the tangent and cotangent function is

a) 0 < y < inf   b) -inf < y < 0   c) -1 <= y <= 1   d) -inf < y < inf

Answer: d) -inf < y < inf

Worked Example: 1(vi). If f(-x) = -f(x) then the function is;

a) even   b) odd   c) algebraic   d) periodic

Answer: b) odd

Worked Example: 1(vii). 1 + tan^2(-theta) is;

a) cosec^2(theta)   b) sec^2(theta)   c) cos^2(theta)   d) sin^2(theta)

Answer: b) sec^2(theta)

Worked Example: 1(viii). If y = sin(x) then its domain is;

a) -inf < x < 0   b) 0 < x < inf   c) -inf < x < inf   d) none of these

Answer: c) -inf < x < inf

Worked Example: 1(ix). The period of sec(x) is;

a) pi   b) 2pi   c) 3pi   d) 4pi

Answer: b) 2pi

Worked Example: 1(x). The minimum value of (a + b cos(theta)) is;

a) a + |b|   b) |a| + |b|   c) a - |b|   d) |a| - |b|

Answer: c) a - |b|

Worked Example: 2. Find the maximum and minimum value of the each of the following functions. (i) y = 5 - 7cos(theta); (ii) y = 4 + 3sin(2theta - 5).

Formula used: See the formulas in the Unit 10 Overview and Lessons 1 to 4 of this unit.

Step 1: (i) cos ranges over [-1, 1]: max = 5 + 7 = 12, min = 5 - 7 = -2.

Step 2: (ii) sin ranges over [-1, 1]: max = 4 + 3 = 7, min = 4 - 3 = 1.

Answer: (i) max 12, min -2; (ii) max 7, min 1

Worked Example: 3. Sketch the graph of y = 2sin(x), 0 <= x <= 2pi. (Flag: a sketch question — the graph is described exactly by its key points.)

Formula used: See the formulas in the Unit 10 Overview and Lessons 1 to 4 of this unit.

Step 1: Amplitude 2, period 2pi. Key points: (0, 0), (pi/2, 2), (pi, 0), (3pi/2, -2), (2pi, 0). Join with a smooth wave through these points.

Answer: Sine wave of amplitude 2 on [0, 2pi] (sketch described)

mcqs.q: The range of both the sine and cosine functions is:
mcqs.why: Sine and cosine outputs always lie between -1 and 1 inclusive, and both end values are attained, so the range is -1 <= y <= 1, i.e. the interval [-1, 1].

mcqs.q: If f(-x) = f(x) for all x, then the function is:
mcqs.why: By definition a function with f(-x) = f(x) is an even function; its graph is symmetric about the y-axis. Cosine and secant are the standard examples in this unit.

mcqs.q: If f(x + p) = f(x) for all x, then the function is:
mcqs.why: By definition a function satisfying f(x + p) = f(x) repeats after the shift p and is called periodic; the smallest such positive p is its period.

mcqs.q: The period of tan(x) is:
mcqs.why: Tangent repeats after pi: tan(theta + k pi) = tan(theta) for every integer k, and no smaller positive shift works, so the period of tan(x) is pi (unlike sin and cos, whose period is 2pi).

mcqs.q: The range of both the tangent and cotangent functions is:
mcqs.why: Tangent and cotangent each take every real value: as x approaches an asymptote the values run to -inf and +inf, so the range is -inf < y < inf, all real numbers.

mcqs.q: If f(-x) = -f(x) for all x, then the function is:
mcqs.why: By definition a function with f(-x) = -f(x) is an odd function; its graph has half-turn symmetry about the origin. Sine, tangent, cotangent and cosecant are the examples in this unit.

mcqs.q: 1 + tan^2(-theta) equals:
mcqs.why: Tangent is odd, so tan(-theta) = -tan(theta), and squaring removes the sign: tan^2(-theta) = tan^2(theta). Then the identity 1 + tan^2(theta) = sec^2(theta) gives the result.

mcqs.q: If y = sin(x), then its domain is:
mcqs.why: Sine is defined for every real angle, so its domain is -inf < x < inf, all real numbers. The restriction -1 <= y <= 1 describes its range, not its domain.

mcqs.q: The period of sec(x) is:
mcqs.why: sec(x) = 1/cos(x) repeats exactly when cos(x) repeats. Since cos has period 2pi, sec(theta + 2k pi) = sec(theta) and the period of sec(x) is 2pi.

mcqs.q: Find the maximum value of y = 5 - 7 cos(theta).
mcqs.why: cos(theta) ranges over [-1, 1]. y is largest when cos(theta) = -1: maximum = 5 - 7(-1) = 5 + 7 = 12. (The minimum, at cos(theta) = 1, is 5 - 7 = -2.)

lessons.title: Unit 11 Overview — Inverse Trigonometric Function
lessons.notes_html:
The inverse trigonometric functions undo the ratios, but only on a chosen branch: Sin^(-1) returns an angle in [-pi/2, pi/2], Cos^(-1) one in [0, pi], Tan^(-1) one in (-pi/2, pi/2). So Sin^(-1)(sin(theta)) equals theta only when theta is in that range.

Values are found from the standard triangles (30-60-90 and 45-45-90) and from a drawn right-angled triangle for a given ratio; sums are handled by the addition formulas, above all Tan^(-1) x + Tan^(-1) y = Tan^(-1)((x + y) / (1 - xy)).

Formula: Ranges: Sin^(-1) x in [-pi/2, pi/2]; Cos^(-1) x in [0, pi]; Tan^(-1) x in (-pi/2, pi/2)

Formula: Sin^(-1) x + Cos^(-1) x = pi / 2

Formula: Tan^(-1) x + Tan^(-1) y = Tan^(-1) ((x + y) / (1 - x y)) (for x y < 1)

Formula: 2 Tan^(-1) x = Tan^(-1) (2x / (1 - x^2))

Formula: Sin^(-1) x + Sin^(-1) y = Sin^(-1) (x √(1 - y^2) + y √(1 - x^2))

Key Points

  • Domains: Sin^(-1) and Cos^(-1) need -1 to 1; Tan^(-1) accepts every real x.
  • To evaluate Cos(Sin^(-1)(p)) and the like, draw the triangle: angle with the given ratio, then read the asked ratio.
  • Sec^(-1)(1) = 0 and Cosec^(-1)(1) = pi/2 — boundary values are worth memorising.
  • When an addition formula gives an angle outside the branch range, adjust by ± pi — the solved examples show where the book’s printed equality needs that care.

mcqs.q: What is the principal value range of Sin^(-1) x?
mcqs.why: By definition in the notes, Sin^(-1) returns an angle in [-pi/2, pi/2]; the endpoints are included because sin(+/-pi/2) = +/-1 is defined.

mcqs.q: What is the principal value range of Cos^(-1) x?
mcqs.why: The notes state Cos^(-1) returns one angle in [0, pi]; on this interval cosine decreases from 1 to -1, giving a single value for each x in [-1, 1].

mcqs.q: What is the principal value range of Tan^(-1) x?
mcqs.why: Tan^(-1) is defined in the notes with range (-pi/2, pi/2), open at the ends because tan is undefined at +/-pi/2.

mcqs.q: For -1 <= x <= 1, Sin^(-1) x + Cos^(-1) x equals:
mcqs.why: Formula from the notes: Sin^(-1) x + Cos^(-1) x = pi/2. Check with x=0: Sin^(-1)0=0 and Cos^(-1)0=pi/2, sum = 0+pi/2 = pi/2.

mcqs.q: For xy < 1, Tan^(-1) x + Tan^(-1) y equals:
mcqs.why: Addition formula from the notes: Tan^(-1) x + Tan^(-1) y = Tan^(-1)((x+y)/(1-xy)) for xy<1, so no +/-pi branch correction is needed.

mcqs.q: 2 Tan^(-1) x is equal to:
mcqs.why: Put y=x in the addition formula: Tan^(-1)x+Tan^(-1)x = Tan^(-1)((x+x)/(1-x*x)) = Tan^(-1)(2x/(1-x^2)), as listed in the notes.

mcqs.q: The domain of Sin^(-1) x and Cos^(-1) x is:
mcqs.why: The notes state Sin^(-1) and Cos^(-1) need -1 to 1, because sin and cos never take values outside [-1,1]; Tan^(-1) by contrast accepts every real x.

mcqs.q: The value of Sec^(-1)(1) is:
mcqs.why: Sec^(-1)(1) is the angle in the secant branch with sec = 1. Since sec(0)=1/cos(0)=1/1=1, the value is 0, a boundary value noted in the overview.

mcqs.q: The value of Cosec^(-1)(1) is:
mcqs.why: Cosec^(-1)(1) needs sin = 1/1 = 1 in the cosecant branch. Since sin(pi/2)=1, Cosec^(-1)(1)=pi/2, a boundary value noted in the overview.

mcqs.q: Sin^(-1)(sin(theta)) equals theta only when:
mcqs.why: The notes stress the branch: Sin^(-1) can only return values in [-pi/2, pi/2], so Sin^(-1)(sin theta)=theta holds only when theta itself lies in that range.

lessons.title: Exercise 11.1 (p.340) - Values of Inverse Trigonometric Functions
lessons.notes_html:
Exact values without tables: read the angle whose sine, cosine, tangent, cotangent, secant or cosecant is given, staying inside the branch range; then composite values such as Cos(Sin^(-1)(√(3)/2)) from a drawn triangle; and the graphs of three inverse functions, described by their key points.

In this exercise: 1. Without using tables / calculator, find the value of. 2. Without using tables / calculator, find the value of. 3. Find the value of each of the following. 4. Without using tables / calculator, show that. 5. Draw the graph of the following functions.

Worked Example: 1. Without using tables / calculator, find the value of; (i) Sin^(-1)(1/√(2)); (ii) Sin^(-1)(-1/2); (iii) Cos^(-1)(-1/√(2)); (iv) Cos^(-1)(1/2); (v) Tan^(-1)(1/√(3)); (vi) Tan^(-1)(-1).

Formula used: Sin^(-1)(1/√(2)) = pi/4; Cos^(-1)(1/2) = pi/3; Tan^(-1)(√(3)) = pi/3; for composites, set the inner inverse equal to an angle and draw its triangle.

Step 1: Principal values: (i) Sin^(-1)(1/√(2)) = pi/4. (ii) Sin^(-1)(-1/2) = -pi/6. (iii) Cos^(-1)(-1/√(2)) = 3pi/4. (iv) Cos^(-1)(1/2) = pi/3. (v) Tan^(-1)(1/√(3)) = pi/6. (vi) Tan^(-1)(-1) = -pi/4.

Answer: (i) pi/4; (ii) -pi/6; (iii) 3pi/4; (iv) pi/3; (v) pi/6; (vi) -pi/4

Worked Example: 2. Without using tables / calculator, find the value of; (i) Cot^(-1)(1/√(3)); (ii) Cot^(-1)(-1); (iii) Sec^(-1)(2); (iv) Sec^(-1)(1); (v) Cosec^(-1)(-2/√(3)); (vi) Cosec^(-1)(-1).

Formula used: Sin^(-1)(1/√(2)) = pi/4; Cos^(-1)(1/2) = pi/3; Tan^(-1)(√(3)) = pi/3; for composites, set the inner inverse equal to an angle and draw its triangle.

Step 1: (i) Cot^(-1)(1/√(3)) = pi/3, since cot(pi/3) = 1/√(3). (ii) Cot^(-1)(-1) = 3pi/4. (iii) Sec^(-1)(2) = pi/3, since sec(pi/3) = 2. (iv) Sec^(-1)(1) = 0. (v) Cosec^(-1)(-2/√(3)) = -pi/3, since sin(-pi/3) = -√(3)/2. (vi) Cosec^(-1)(-1) = -pi/2.

Answer: (i) pi/3; (ii) 3pi/4; (iii) pi/3; (iv) 0; (v) -pi/3; (vi) -pi/2

Worked Example: 4. Without using tables / calculator, show that; (i) Tan^(-1)(12/5) = Cot^(-1)(5/12); (ii) Tan^(-1)(√(3)) = Sin^(-1)(√(3)/2); (iii) Cosec^(-1)(2/√(3)) = Cos^(-1)(1/2); (iv) Cos^(-1)(4/9) = Cot^(-1)(4/√(65)).

Formula used: Sin^(-1)(1/√(2)) = pi/4; Cos^(-1)(1/2) = pi/3; Tan^(-1)(√(3)) = pi/3; for composites, set the inner inverse equal to an angle and draw its triangle.

Step 1: (i) If tan(theta) = 12/5 with theta in (0, pi/2), then cot(theta) = 5/12, so theta = Cot^(-1)(5/12).

Step 2: (ii) Tan^(-1)(√(3)) = pi/3 = Sin^(-1)(√(3)/2).

Step 3: (iii) Cosec^(-1)(2/√(3)) = pi/3 = Cos^(-1)(1/2).

Step 4: (iv) Let theta = Cos^(-1)(4/9). Then sin(theta) = √(1 - 16/81) = √(65)/9, so cot(theta) = (4/9)/(√(65)/9) = 4/√(65). Hence theta = Cot^(-1)(4/√(65)).

Answer: All four identities proved

Worked Example: 5. Draw the graph of the following functions. (i) y = Sin^(-1)(x) for -1 <= x <= 1; (ii) y = Cot^(-1)(x) for -inf < x < inf; (iii) y = Sec^(-1)(x) for -inf < x < inf. (Flag: sketch questions — each graph is described exactly by its key points and branches.)

Formula used: Sin^(-1)(1/√(2)) = pi/4; Cos^(-1)(1/2) = pi/3; Tan^(-1)(√(3)) = pi/3; for composites, set the inner inverse equal to an angle and draw its triangle.

Step 1: (i) y = Sin^(-1)(x): increasing curve through (-1, -pi/2), (-0.5, -pi/6), (0, 0), (0.5, pi/6), (1, pi/2); steep (vertical tangent) at x = +/-1.

Step 2: (ii) y = Cot^(-1)(x): decreasing curve from pi (as x -> -inf) to 0 (as x -> +inf), through (0, pi/2), (1, pi/4), (-1, 3pi/4).

Step 3: (iii) y = Sec^(-1)(x): defined for |x| >= 1. Branch on [1, inf): from (1, 0) rising towards pi/2 as x -> inf. Branch on (-inf, -1]: from (-1, pi) falling towards pi/2 as x -> -inf.

Answer: Graphs described by key points (flag: sketch questions — see steps)

mcqs.q: Sin^(-1)(1/sqrt(2)) equals:
mcqs.why: Find angle in [-pi/2, pi/2] with sine 1/sqrt(2). sin(pi/4)=1/sqrt(2) and pi/4 is in the range, so Sin^(-1)(1/sqrt(2))=pi/4.

mcqs.q: Sin^(-1)(-1/2) equals:
mcqs.why: Find angle in [-pi/2, pi/2] with sine -1/2. sin(-pi/6)=-sin(pi/6)=-1/2, and -pi/6 is in the range, so the value is -pi/6.

mcqs.q: Cos^(-1)(-1/sqrt(2)) equals:
mcqs.why: Find angle in [0, pi] with cosine -1/sqrt(2). cos(3pi/4)=-cos(pi/4)=-1/sqrt(2), and 3pi/4 is in [0, pi], so the value is 3pi/4.

mcqs.q: Cos^(-1)(1/2) equals:
mcqs.why: Find angle in [0, pi] with cosine 1/2. cos(pi/3)=1/2, so Cos^(-1)(1/2)=pi/3, as given in the worked examples.

mcqs.q: Tan^(-1)(1/sqrt(3)) equals:
mcqs.why: Find angle in (-pi/2, pi/2) with tangent 1/sqrt(3). tan(pi/6)=1/sqrt(3), so Tan^(-1)(1/sqrt(3))=pi/6.

mcqs.q: Tan^(-1)(-1) equals:
mcqs.why: Find angle in (-pi/2, pi/2) with tangent -1. tan(-pi/4)=-tan(pi/4)=-1, so Tan^(-1)(-1)=-pi/4; 3pi/4 is outside the Tan^(-1) range.

mcqs.q: Cot^(-1)(1/sqrt(3)) equals:
mcqs.why: cot(pi/3)=cos(pi/3)/sin(pi/3)=(1/2)/(sqrt(3)/2)=1/sqrt(3), and pi/3 lies in the cotangent branch (0, pi), so Cot^(-1)(1/sqrt(3))=pi/3.

mcqs.q: Sec^(-1)(2) equals:
mcqs.why: sec(theta)=2 means cos(theta)=1/2. In the secant branch, theta=pi/3 gives cos(pi/3)=1/2, so sec(pi/3)=2 and Sec^(-1)(2)=pi/3.

mcqs.q: Cosec^(-1)(-1) equals:
mcqs.why: Cosec^(-1)(-1) needs sin = -1. sin(-pi/2)=-1 and -pi/2 is the lower endpoint of the cosecant branch, so Cosec^(-1)(-1)=-pi/2.

mcqs.q: If theta = Cos^(-1)(4/9), then Cot^(-1) form of theta is Cot^(-1) of:
mcqs.why: cos theta=4/9, so sin theta=sqrt(1-16/81)=sqrt(65)/9. Then cot theta=cos/sin=(4/9)/(sqrt(65)/9)=4/sqrt(65), hence theta=Cot^(-1)(4/sqrt(65)).

lessons.title: Exercise 11.2 (p.344) - Addition Formulas for Inverse Functions
lessons.notes_html:
Eighteen proofs that sums of inverse functions equal a single inverse value (or pi/4, pi/2). The engine is the Tan^(-1) and Cos^(-1) addition formulas. Two printed questions are defective — an impossible Cos^(-1)(104/85) and a wrong sign — and the solved notes prove the corrected statements and say exactly what was wrong.

In this exercise: 1. Prove: Sin^(-1)(7/25) + Sin^(-1)(5/13) = Cos^(-1)(253/325). 2. Prove: Tan^(-1)(1/6) + Tan^(-1)(1/7) = Tan^(-1)(13/41). 3. Prove: 2Tan^(-1)(2/3) = Cos^(-1)(5/13). 4. Prove: Cos^(-1)(2/√(5)) + Tan^(-1)(1/3) = pi/4. 5. Prove: Cos^(-1)(3/5) - Cos^(-1)(8/17) = Cos^(-1)(104/85). 6. Prove: Sin^(-1)(77/85) + Sin^(-1)(3/5) = Cos^(-1)(87/425). 7. Prove: Cos^(-1)(63/65) + 2Tan^(-1)(1/5) = Cos^(-1)(4/5). 8. Prove: Tan^(-1)(3/4) + Tan^(-1)(3/5) - Tan^(-1)(8/19) = pi/4. 9. Prove: Sec^(-1)(√(5)/2) + Cot^(-1)(3) = pi/4. 10. Prove: Cos^(-1)(3/5) + Cos^(-1)(12/13) + Cos^(-1)(63/65) = pi/2. 11. Prove: 2Tan^(-1)(1/3) + Tan^(-1)(1/7) = pi/4. 12. Prove: Tan^(-1)(1/3) + Tan^(-1)(1/2) = Tan^(-1)(1/11) + Tan^(-1)(5/6). 13. Show that Sin(Cos^(-1)(y)) = √(1 - y^2). 14. Show that Tan^(-1)(y) + Tan^(-1)(-y) = 0. 15. Show that Cos^(-1)(y) + Cos^(-1)(-y) = pi. 16. Show that Tan(Cos^(-1)(y)) = √(1 - y^2)/y. 17. Show that Sin(2Cos^(-1)(y)) = 2y √(1 - y^2). 18. Show that Cos(2Sin^(-1)(y)) = 1 - 2y^2.

Worked Example: 1. Prove: Sin^(-1)(7/25) + Sin^(-1)(5/13) = Cos^(-1)(253/325).

Formula used: Tan^(-1) x + Tan^(-1) y = Tan^(-1)((x + y) / (1 - xy)); Cos^(-1) x - Cos^(-1) y and Sin^(-1) sums by the matching formulas; 2 Tan^(-1) x = Cos^(-1)((1 - x^2) / (1 + x^2)).

Step 1: Let A = Sin^(-1)(7/25), B = Sin^(-1)(5/13). Then cos(A) = 24/25, cos(B) = 12/13.

Step 2: Cos(A + B) = cos(A)cos(B) - sin(A)sin(B) = (24 x 12 - 7 x 5)/(25 x 13) = 253/325.

Step 3: Since A + B is in (0, pi), A + B = Cos^(-1)(253/325).

Answer: Cos^(-1)(253/325) is proved

Worked Example: 4. Prove: Cos^(-1)(2/√(5)) + Tan^(-1)(1/3) = pi/4.

Formula used: Tan^(-1) x + Tan^(-1) y = Tan^(-1)((x + y) / (1 - xy)); Cos^(-1) x - Cos^(-1) y and Sin^(-1) sums by the matching formulas; 2 Tan^(-1) x = Cos^(-1)((1 - x^2) / (1 + x^2)).

Step 1: Let A = Cos^(-1)(2/√(5)). Then sin(A) = 1/√(5) and tan(A) = 1/2.

Step 2: Tan^(-1)(1/2) + Tan^(-1)(1/3) = Tan^(-1)((1/2 + 1/3)/(1 - 1/6)) = Tan^(-1)(1) = pi/4.

Answer: pi/4 is proved

Worked Example: 8. Prove: Tan^(-1)(3/4) + Tan^(-1)(3/5) - Tan^(-1)(8/19) = pi/4.

Formula used: Tan^(-1) x + Tan^(-1) y = Tan^(-1)((x + y) / (1 - xy)); Cos^(-1) x - Cos^(-1) y and Sin^(-1) sums by the matching formulas; 2 Tan^(-1) x = Cos^(-1)((1 - x^2) / (1 + x^2)).

Step 1: Tan^(-1)(3/4) + Tan^(-1)(3/5) = Tan^(-1)((3/4 + 3/5)/(1 - 9/20)) = Tan^(-1)(27/11).

Step 2: Tan^(-1)(27/11) - Tan^(-1)(8/19) = Tan^(-1)((27/11 - 8/19)/(1 + 216/209)) = Tan^(-1)(425/425) = Tan^(-1)(1) = pi/4.

Answer: pi/4 is proved

Worked Example: 11. Prove: 2Tan^(-1)(1/3) + Tan^(-1)(1/7) = pi/4.

Formula used: Tan^(-1) x + Tan^(-1) y = Tan^(-1)((x + y) / (1 - xy)); Cos^(-1) x - Cos^(-1) y and Sin^(-1) sums by the matching formulas; 2 Tan^(-1) x = Cos^(-1)((1 - x^2) / (1 + x^2)).

Step 1: 2Tan^(-1)(1/3) = Tan^(-1)((2/3)/(1 - 1/9)) = Tan^(-1)(3/4).

Step 2: Tan^(-1)(3/4) + Tan^(-1)(1/7) = Tan^(-1)((3/4 + 1/7)/(1 - 3/28)) = Tan^(-1)(1) = pi/4.

Answer: pi/4 is proved

Worked Example: 15. Show that Cos^(-1)(y) + Cos^(-1)(-y) = pi.

Formula used: Tan^(-1) x + Tan^(-1) y = Tan^(-1)((x + y) / (1 - xy)); Cos^(-1) x - Cos^(-1) y and Sin^(-1) sums by the matching formulas; 2 Tan^(-1) x = Cos^(-1)((1 - x^2) / (1 + x^2)).

Step 1: Cos^(-1)(-y) = pi - Cos^(-1)(y), since cos(pi - theta) = -cos(theta). Hence the sum is pi.

Answer: pi is proved

Worked Example: 18. Show that Cos(2Sin^(-1)(y)) = 1 - 2y^2.

Formula used: Tan^(-1) x + Tan^(-1) y = Tan^(-1)((x + y) / (1 - xy)); Cos^(-1) x - Cos^(-1) y and Sin^(-1) sums by the matching formulas; 2 Tan^(-1) x = Cos^(-1)((1 - x^2) / (1 + x^2)).

Step 1: Let theta = Sin^(-1)(y). Then Cos(2theta) = 1 - 2sin^2(theta) = 1 - 2y^2.

Answer: 1 - 2y^2 is proved

mcqs.q: 2 Tan^(-1)(2/3) equals:
Cos^(-1)(2/sqrt(5)) + Tan^(-1)(1/3) equals:
The printed statement Cos^(-1)(3/5) - Cos^(-1)(8/17) = Cos^(-1)(104/85) is defective because:
options: 3/5 is outside the domain of Cos^(-1)
A difference of Cos^(-1) values is always negative
mcqs.why: Cos^(-1) is defined only for inputs in [-1,1]. Here 104/85 is about 1.22 > 1, so Cos^(-1)(104/85) is impossible; the notes flag this printed question as defective.

mcqs.q: For any y in [-1, 1], Cos^(-1)(y) + Cos^(-1)(-y) equals:
mcqs.why: Cos^(-1)(-y)=pi-Cos^(-1)(y) because cos(pi-theta)=-cos(theta). Adding: Cos^(-1)(y)+pi-Cos^(-1)(y)=pi, as shown in the notes.

mcqs.q: For any real y, Tan^(-1)(y) + Tan^(-1)(-y) equals:
mcqs.why: Tan^(-1) is an odd function: Tan^(-1)(-y)=-Tan^(-1)(y) because tan is odd. Hence the sum is Tan^(-1)(y)-Tan^(-1)(y)=0.

mcqs.q: Cos(2 Sin^(-1)(y)) equals:
mcqs.why: Let theta=Sin^(-1)(y), so sin theta=y. Cos(2theta)=1-2sin^2(theta) by the double-angle formula = 1-2y^2 after substitution.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 11 (pp.345-347)
lessons.notes_html:
Review of Unit 11: domains and ranges of the inverse functions, the identity Sin^(-1) x + Cos^(-1) x = pi/2, and composite values.

In this exercise: 1. Choose the correct options. 2. Find the value of each of the following. 3. Show that; Tan^(-1)(12/5) = Sin^(-1)(12/13). 4. Prove that; Sin^(-1)(1/√(5)) + Cot^(-1)(3) = pi/4. 5. Prove: Sin^(-1)(4/5) + Sin^(-1)(5/13) + Sin^(-1)(16/65) = pi/2.

Worked Example: 1(i). Domain of the following y = Sin^(-1)(x) is;

a) [-1, 1]   b) (-inf, inf)   c) [0, pi]   d) [-pi/2, pi/2]

Answer: a) [-1, 1]

Worked Example: 1(ii). Range of the function y = Cos^(-1)(x) is

a) [pi/2, -pi/2]   b) [pi, 0]   c) [0, pi]   d) [-pi, pi]

Answer: c) [0, pi]

Worked Example: 1(iii). Domain of y = Tan^(-1)(x) is

a) [-pi/2, pi/2]   b) (0, pi)   c) [-1, 1]   d) [-inf, inf]

Answer: d) [-inf, inf]

Worked Example: 1(iv). Which point lies on the graph of y = Sin^(-1)(x)?

a) (1, pi)   b) (0.5, pi/6)   c) (1, pi/2)   d) (2, pi/2)

Answer: c) (1, pi/2)

Note: Options (b) (0.5, pi/6) and (c) (1, pi/2) both lie on the graph; the book ticks (c).

Worked Example: 1(v). Which function has a graph that passes through (0, pi/2)

a) y = Cos^(-1)(x)   b) y = Tan^(-1)(x)   c) y = Sec^(-1)(x)   d) y = Sin^(-1)(x)

Answer: a) y = Cos^(-1)(x)

Worked Example: 1(vi). Sin^(-1)(x) + Cos^(-1)(x) is equal to;

a) pi/2   b) pi   c) 0   d) undefined

Answer: a) pi/2

Worked Example: 1(vii). Sin^(-1)(1/2) + Cos^(-1)(1/2) is equal to;

a) 0   b) pi   c) pi/2   d) pi/4

Answer: c) pi/2

Worked Example: 1(viii). Tan^(-1)(1) + Tan^(-1)(√(3)) is equal to;

a) pi/6   b) pi/3   c) pi/2   d) 7pi/12

Answer: d) 7pi/12

Worked Example: 2. Find the value of each of the following. (i) Sin[Cos^(-1)(√(3)/2)]; (ii) Sec[Cosec^(-1)(2)]; (iii) Cosec[Tan^(-1)(1)]; (iv) Sec[Sin^(-1)(1/√(2))].

Formula used: See the formulas in the Unit 11 Overview and Lessons 1 to 2 of this unit.

Step 1: (i) Cos^(-1)(√(3)/2) = pi/6, so Sin(pi/6) = 1/2.

Step 2: (ii) Cosec^(-1)(2) = pi/6, so Sec(pi/6) = 2/√(3).

Step 3: (iii) Tan^(-1)(1) = pi/4, so Cosec(pi/4) = √(2).

Step 4: (iv) Sin^(-1)(1/√(2)) = pi/4, so Sec(pi/4) = √(2).

Answer: (i) 1/2; (ii) 2/√(3); (iii) √(2); (iv) √(2)

Worked Example: 3. Show that; Tan^(-1)(12/5) = Sin^(-1)(12/13).

Formula used: See the formulas in the Unit 11 Overview and Lessons 1 to 2 of this unit.

Step 1: Let theta = Tan^(-1)(12/5), with theta in (0, pi/2). Then tan(theta) = 12/5, so sin(theta) = 12/13 (from the 5-12-13 triangle). Hence theta = Sin^(-1)(12/13).

Answer: Sin^(-1)(12/13) is proved

Worked Example: 4. Prove that; Sin^(-1)(1/√(5)) + Cot^(-1)(3) = pi/4.

Formula used: See the formulas in the Unit 11 Overview and Lessons 1 to 2 of this unit.

Step 1: Sin^(-1)(1/√(5)) = Tan^(-1)(1/2), since sin = 1/√(5) and cos = 2/√(5). Cot^(-1)(3) = Tan^(-1)(1/3).

Step 2: Sum = Tan^(-1)(1/2) + Tan^(-1)(1/3) = Tan^(-1)((5/6)/(5/6)) = pi/4.

Answer: pi/4 is proved

Worked Example: 5. Prove: Sin^(-1)(4/5) + Sin^(-1)(5/13) + Sin^(-1)(16/65) = pi/2.

Formula used: See the formulas in the Unit 11 Overview and Lessons 1 to 2 of this unit.

Step 1: Let S = Sin^(-1)(4/5) + Sin^(-1)(5/13). Then sin(S) = (4 x 12 + 3 x 5)/65 = 63/65 and cos(S) = (3 x 12 - 4 x 5)/65 = 16/65.

Step 2: Let T = Sin^(-1)(16/65), so sin(T) = 16/65, cos(T) = 63/65. Then sin(S + T) = (63 x 63 + 16 x 16)/4225 = 1. Since S + T is in (0, pi), S + T = pi/2.

Answer: pi/2 is proved

mcqs.q: The domain of y = Sin^(-1)(x) is:
mcqs.why: Sin^(-1) reverses sine, whose values lie in [-1,1], so its domain is [-1,1]. The interval [-pi/2, pi/2] is its range, not its domain.

mcqs.q: The range of y = Cos^(-1)(x) is:
mcqs.why: By definition Cos^(-1) returns angles in [0, pi]; this is the review answer (c). The domain [-1,1] must not be confused with the range.

mcqs.q: The domain of y = Tan^(-1)(x) is:
mcqs.why: Tangent takes every real value, so Tan^(-1) accepts every real x: domain (-inf, inf), review answer (d). Its range is (-pi/2, pi/2).

mcqs.q: Which point lies on the graph of y = Sin^(-1)(x) as ticked in the book?
mcqs.why: Sin^(-1)(1)=pi/2 because sin(pi/2)=1, so (1, pi/2) is on the graph. Note (0.5, pi/6) also lies on it, but the book ticks (1, pi/2).

mcqs.q: Which function has a graph passing through (0, pi/2)?
mcqs.why: Cos^(-1)(0)=pi/2 because cos(pi/2)=0, so y=Cos^(-1)(x) passes through (0, pi/2). Sin^(-1)(0)=0 and Tan^(-1)(0)=0 do not.

mcqs.q: Sin^(-1)(x) + Cos^(-1)(x) is equal to:
mcqs.why: Identity from the review: Sin^(-1)x+Cos^(-1)x=pi/2 for x in [-1,1]. Check x=1: pi/2+0=pi/2, confirming the identity.

mcqs.q: Sin^(-1)(1/2) + Cos^(-1)(1/2) is equal to:
mcqs.why: Apply Sin^(-1)x+Cos^(-1)x=pi/2 with x=1/2: directly the sum is pi/2. Separately Sin^(-1)(1/2)=pi/6 and Cos^(-1)(1/2)=pi/3, and pi/6+pi/3=pi/2.

mcqs.q: Tan^(-1)(1) + Tan^(-1)(sqrt(3)) is equal to:
mcqs.why: Tan^(-1)(1)=pi/4 (tan pi/4=1) and Tan^(-1)(sqrt(3))=pi/3 (tan pi/3=sqrt(3)). Sum = pi/4+pi/3 = (3pi+4pi)/12 = 7pi/12.

mcqs.q: Sin[Cos^(-1)(sqrt(3)/2)] equals:
mcqs.why: Cos^(-1)(sqrt(3)/2)=pi/6 because cos(pi/6)=sqrt(3)/2. Then Sin(pi/6)=1/2, so the composite value is 1/2.

mcqs.q: Tan^(-1)(12/5) equals which Sin^(-1) value?
mcqs.why: Let theta=Tan^(-1)(12/5) in (0,pi/2); tan=12/5 gives the 5-12-13 triangle, so sin theta=12/13. Hence theta=Sin^(-1)(12/13).

lessons.title: Unit 12 Overview — Solution of Trigonometric Equations
lessons.notes_html:
Solving sin(theta) = k starts from one principal value alpha and then writes every solution: for sine, theta = n pi + (-1)^n alpha; for cosine, theta = 2n pi ± alpha; for tangent, theta = n pi + alpha (n any integer). In a fixed interval, list the values of n that land inside it.

Harder equations are first reduced to one function — using sin^2 + cos^2 = 1, sec^2 = 1 + tan^2, or a double-angle formula — then factorised. Roots that make any original term undefined (for example where tan or sec does not exist) must be rejected.

Formula: sin(theta) = sin(alpha) → theta = n pi + (-1)^n alpha

Formula: cos(theta) = cos(alpha) → theta = 2n pi ± alpha

Formula: tan(theta) = tan(alpha) → theta = n pi + alpha

Formula: sin(theta) = 0 → theta = n pi; cos(theta) = 0 → theta = (2n + 1) pi / 2; sin(theta) = 1 → theta = 2n pi + pi / 2

Formula: Quadratic in one ratio: solve for sin(theta) (or cos, tan), reject any value outside [-1, 1] for sin and cos

Key Points

  • Always state the interval first — a general solution and an interval solution are different answers.
  • After squaring or multiplying through, check every root in the original equation; extraneous roots do occur in this unit.
  • cosec(theta) = k means sin(theta) = 1/k — and |k| must be at least 1, otherwise there is no solution.
  • For graph solutions on [-pi/2, pi/2], the answer is where the curve meets the line — read it off and verify by substitution.

mcqs.q: If sin(theta) = sin(alpha), the general solution is:
mcqs.why: Formula from the overview: sin theta = sin alpha gives theta = n pi + (-1)^n alpha for any integer n, covering both the I and II quadrant families.

mcqs.q: If cos(theta) = cos(alpha), the general solution is:
mcqs.why: Formula from the overview: cos theta = cos alpha gives theta = 2n pi +/- alpha for any integer n, because cosine repeats every 2pi with symmetric solutions.

mcqs.q: If tan(theta) = tan(alpha), the general solution is:
mcqs.why: Formula from the overview: tan theta = tan alpha gives theta = n pi + alpha, because tangent has period pi, so one family with step pi suffices.

mcqs.q: The general solution of sin(theta) = 0 is:
mcqs.why: sin theta=0 at theta=0, pi, 2pi, ... and negatives, i.e. every multiple of pi: theta=n pi. This is listed directly in the overview formulas.

mcqs.q: The general solution of cos(theta) = 0 is:
mcqs.why: cos theta=0 at odd multiples of pi/2: pi/2, 3pi/2, ... Hence theta=(2n+1)pi/2 for integer n, as listed in the overview.

mcqs.q: The general solution of sin(theta) = 1 is:
mcqs.why: sin theta=1 only at pi/2 plus full turns: theta=2n pi+pi/2. The form (2n+1)pi/2 would also include 3pi/2 where sin=-1, so it is wrong.

mcqs.q: The equation cosec(theta) = k can have a solution only if:
mcqs.why: cosec theta = k means sin theta = 1/k. Since |sin theta|<=1, need |1/k|<=1, i.e. |k|>=1; otherwise there is no solution, as the overview warns.

mcqs.q: When solving a trigonometric equation, a root where tan or sec is undefined must be:
mcqs.why: The overview states roots that make any original term undefined (for example where tan or sec does not exist) must be rejected, even if they satisfy the reduced equation.

mcqs.q: In a quadratic in sin(theta), a value of sin(theta) outside [-1, 1] must be:
mcqs.why: The overview rule: solve for sin theta (or cos, tan), reject any value outside [-1,1] for sin and cos, since sine and cosine never exceed 1 in magnitude.

mcqs.q: For a graph solution on [-pi/2, pi/2], the solution is found where:
options: The curve meets the x-axis only
mcqs.why: The overview states: for graph solutions the answer is where the curve meets the line — read it off and verify by substitution into the original equation.

lessons.title: Exercise 12.1 (p.353) - Basic Equations and Graphical Solutions
lessons.notes_html:
The first nine equations are the basic types sin(theta) = k, cos(theta) = k, tan(theta) = k and their cosec, sec and cot partners. The last four are solved from a graph on -pi/2 to pi/2, where the curve meets a straight line.

In this exercise: 1. Find solutions of the trigonometric equations. 1. sin(theta) = 1/2; 2. cos(theta) = -1/√(2); 3. tan(theta) = √(3); 4. sin(theta) = -√(3)/2; 5. cos(theta) = 1; 6. tan(theta) = -1; 7. 2. By using graph, find the solution of the following equations for -pi/2 <= theta <= pi/2. 10. 2sin(theta) - theta = 0; 11. cos(theta) = 1 + theta; 12. sin(theta) = theta; 13. cos(theta) = theta/2.

Worked Example: 1-9. Find solutions of the trigonometric equations. 1. sin(theta) = 1/2; 2. cos(theta) = -1/√(2); 3. tan(theta) = √(3); 4. sin(theta) = -√(3)/2; 5. cos(theta) = 1; 6. tan(theta) = -1; 7. tan(theta) = -1/√(3); 8. cos(theta) = 0; 9. tan(theta) = 1.

Formula used: sin(theta) = sin(alpha): theta = n pi + (-1)^n alpha; cos: theta = 2n pi ± alpha; tan: theta = n pi + alpha; in an interval, take the n values that fit.

Step 1: 1. sin(theta) = 1/2: reference angle pi/6, positive in quadrants I and II: theta = pi/6 + 2n pi, 5pi/6 + 2n pi.

Step 2: 2. cos(theta) = -1/√(2): reference angle pi/4, negative in quadrants II and III: theta = 3pi/4 + 2n pi, 5pi/4 + 2n pi.

Step 3: 3. tan(theta) = √(3): period pi: theta = pi/3 + n pi.

Step 4: 4. sin(theta) = -√(3)/2: reference angle pi/3, negative in quadrants III and IV: theta = 4pi/3 + 2n pi, 5pi/3 + 2n pi.

Step 5: 5. cos(theta) = 1: theta = 2n pi.

Step 6: 6. tan(theta) = -1: theta = -pi/4 + n pi (equivalently 3pi/4 + n pi).

Step 7: 7. tan(theta) = -1/√(3): theta = -pi/6 + n pi.

Step 8: 8. cos(theta) = 0: theta = pi/2 + n pi.

Step 9: 9. tan(theta) = 1: theta = pi/4 + n pi.

Answer: 1. theta = pi/6 + 2n pi, 5pi/6 + 2n pi; 2. theta = 3pi/4 + 2n pi, 5pi/4 + 2n pi; 3. theta = pi/3 + n pi; 4. theta = 4pi/3 + 2n pi, 5pi/3 + 2n pi; 5. theta = 2n pi; 6. theta = -pi/4 + n pi; 7. theta = -pi/6 + n pi; 8. theta = pi/2 + n pi; 9. theta = pi/4 + n pi

Worked Example: 10-13. By using graph, find the solution of the following equations for -pi/2 <= theta <= pi/2. 10. 2sin(theta) - theta = 0; 11. cos(theta) = 1 + theta; 12. sin(theta) = theta; 13. cos(theta) = theta/2. (Flag: Q10-12 have only the trivial solution 0 in this interval; Q13 has one solution, approximately 1.03, found graphically/numerically.)

Formula used: sin(theta) = sin(alpha): theta = n pi + (-1)^n alpha; cos: theta = 2n pi ± alpha; tan: theta = n pi + alpha; in an interval, take the n values that fit.

Step 1: 10. 2sin(theta) = theta, i.e. sin(theta) = theta/2. The graphs of y = sin(theta) and y = theta/2 meet at theta = 0 inside [-pi/2, pi/2]; their other crossings, at about +/-1.895, lie outside this interval. So theta = 0 only.

Step 2: 11. cos(theta) = 1 + theta. At theta = 0 both sides are 1. The function cos(theta) - 1 - theta has derivative -sin(theta) - 1 <= 0 on the interval, so it is decreasing and has no other zero. So theta = 0 only.

Step 3: 12. sin(theta) = theta. Since |sin(theta)| < |theta| for theta not equal to 0, the only solution is theta = 0.

Step 4: 13. cos(theta) = theta/2. On the negative side cos(theta) > 0 > theta/2, so no solution there. On (0, pi/2], cos falls from 1 to 0 while theta/2 rises from 0 to pi/4, so they cross once, at theta about 1.03 (check: cos(1.03) is about 0.515 and 1.03/2 = 0.515).

Answer: 10. theta = 0 only; 11. theta = 0 only; 12. theta = 0 only; 13. theta about 1.03

mcqs.q: The solutions of sin(theta) = 1/2 are:
mcqs.why: Reference angle: sin alpha=1/2 gives alpha=pi/6. Sine is positive in quadrants I and II, so theta=pi/6+2n pi and pi-pi/6=5pi/6+2n pi.

mcqs.q: The solutions of cos(theta) = -1/sqrt(2) are:
mcqs.why: Reference angle pi/4 since cos(pi/4)=1/sqrt(2). Cosine negative in quadrants II and III: pi-pi/4=3pi/4 and pi+pi/4=5pi/4, each +2n pi.

mcqs.q: The solutions of tan(theta) = sqrt(3) are:
mcqs.why: tan(pi/3)=sqrt(3) and tangent has period pi, so by theta=n pi+alpha with alpha=pi/3: theta=pi/3+n pi.

mcqs.q: The solutions of sin(theta) = -sqrt(3)/2 are:
mcqs.why: Reference angle pi/3 since sin(pi/3)=sqrt(3)/2. Sine negative in quadrants III and IV: pi+pi/3=4pi/3 and 2pi-pi/3=5pi/3, each +2n pi.

mcqs.q: The solutions of cos(theta) = 1 are:
mcqs.why: cos theta=1 at theta=0 and every full turn. Using theta=2n pi +/- alpha with alpha=Cos^(-1)(1)=0 gives theta=2n pi.

mcqs.q: The solutions of tan(theta) = -1 are:
mcqs.why: tan(-pi/4)=-1 and tangent period is pi, so theta=n pi+alpha with alpha=-pi/4 gives theta=-pi/4+n pi (equivalently 3pi/4+n pi).

mcqs.q: The solutions of tan(theta) = -1/sqrt(3) are:
mcqs.why: tan(-pi/6)=-tan(pi/6)=-1/sqrt(3). With period pi, theta=-pi/6+n pi gives every solution.

mcqs.q: The solutions of cos(theta) = 0 are:
mcqs.why: cos theta=0 at pi/2, 3pi/2, 5pi/2,... spaced by pi, so theta=pi/2+n pi, which is the same family as (2n+1)pi/2.

mcqs.q: The solutions of tan(theta) = 1 are:
mcqs.why: tan(pi/4)=1 and tangent period is pi, so theta=pi/4+n pi by the formula theta=n pi+alpha with alpha=pi/4.

mcqs.q: On -pi/2 <= theta <= pi/2, the graphical solution of cos(theta) = theta/2 is:
mcqs.why: cos falls from 1 to 0 on (0, pi/2] while theta/2 rises from 0 to pi/4, crossing once. Check theta=1.03: cos(1.03) is about 0.515 and 1.03/2=0.515, so theta is about 1.03.

lessons.title: Exercise 12.2 (p.355) - General Solutions
lessons.notes_html:
Twenty-two equations for the general solution or a solution set: quadratics in tan and cot, equations mixing cosec and cot, and factorisable equations such as tan(x) = 2 sin(x) and cos(2theta) = cos(theta). One equation (cosec(2theta) = 1/2) has no solution at all, and one root in Q21 is extraneous — both are flagged in the working.

In this exercise: 1. Solve each equation giving general solution. 1. cosec(2theta) = 1/2; 2. cos(theta) = -1/2; 3. cosec(3theta/2) = -2; 4. sec^2(theta) = 4/3; 5. 4sin^2(theta) - 1 = 0; 6. sec^2(theta) - 4 = 0. 2. Find the values of theta satisfying the following equations. 7. 3tan^2(theta) + 2√(3)tan(theta) + 1 = 0; 8. cot^2(theta) - cosec(theta) - 1 = 0; 9. 2cos(theta) + sin^2(theta) - 1 = 0; 10. 3. Find the solution sets of the following equation. 13. tan(x) = 2sin(x); 14. 4sin^2(theta/2) - 3 = 0; 15. cos(2theta) = cos(theta); 16. sin(4x) - sin(2x) = cos(3x); 17. sin(x) + cos(3x) = cos(5x); 18.

Worked Example: 1-6. Solve each equation giving general solution. 1. cosec(2theta) = 1/2; 2. cos(theta) = -1/2; 3. cosec(3theta/2) = -2; 4. sec^2(theta) = 4/3; 5. 4sin^2(theta) - 1 = 0; 6. sec^2(theta) - 4 = 0.

Formula used: Reduce to one ratio with sin^2 + cos^2 = 1 or sec^2 = 1 + tan^2; factorise; solve each factor by the general-solution formulas; reject roots outside the domain.

Step 1: 1. cosec(2theta) = 1/2 means sin(2theta) = 2, impossible since |sin| <= 1. NO solution.

Step 2: 2. cos(theta) = -1/2: reference angle pi/3, negative in quadrants II and III: theta = 2pi/3 + 2n pi, 4pi/3 + 2n pi.

Step 3: 3. sin(3theta/2) = -1/2: 3theta/2 = 7pi/6 + 2n pi or 11pi/6 + 2n pi, so theta = 7pi/9 + 4n pi/3, 11pi/9 + 4n pi/3.

Step 4: 4. sec^2(theta) = 4/3 gives cos(theta) = +/-√(3)/2, so theta = +/-pi/6 + n pi.

Step 5: 5. sin^2(theta) = 1/4 gives sin(theta) = +/-1/2, so theta = +/-pi/6 + n pi.

Step 6: 6. sec^2(theta) = 4 gives cos(theta) = +/-1/2, so theta = +/-pi/3 + n pi.

Answer: 1. NO solution; 2. theta = 2pi/3 + 2n pi, 4pi/3 + 2n pi; 3. theta = 7pi/9 + 4n pi/3, 11pi/9 + 4n pi/3; 4. theta = +/-pi/6 + n pi; 5. theta = +/-pi/6 + n pi; 6. theta = +/-pi/3 + n pi

Worked Example: 7-12. Find the values of theta satisfying the following equations. 7. 3tan^2(theta) + 2√(3)tan(theta) + 1 = 0; 8. cot^2(theta) - cosec(theta) - 1 = 0; 9. 2cos(theta) + sin^2(theta) - 1 = 0; 10. 4cos^2(theta) - 8sin(theta) + 1 = 0; 11. (sec(theta) - 2)(2sin(theta) - 1) = 0; 12. (cosec(theta) + 2)(2cos(theta) - 1) = 0. (Values given in [0, 2pi); general forms in the steps.)

Formula used: Reduce to one ratio with sin^2 + cos^2 = 1 or sec^2 = 1 + tan^2; factorise; solve each factor by the general-solution formulas; reject roots outside the domain.

Step 1: 7. (√(3)tan(theta) + 1)^2 = 0, so tan(theta) = -1/√(3): theta = 5pi/6, 11pi/6; generally -pi/6 + n pi.

Step 2: 8. Using cot^2 = cosec^2 - 1: cosec^2(theta) - cosec(theta) - 2 = 0, so cosec(theta) = 2 or -1: theta = pi/6, 5pi/6, 3pi/2.

Step 3: 9. Using sin^2 = 1 - cos^2: cos(theta)(2 - cos(theta)) = 0, so cos(theta) = 0: theta = pi/2, 3pi/2.

Step 4: 10. Using cos^2 = 1 - sin^2: 4sin^2(theta) + 8sin(theta) - 5 = 0, so sin(theta) = 1/2 (the other root -5/2 is impossible): theta = pi/6, 5pi/6.

Step 5: 11. sec(theta) = 2 gives theta = pi/3, 5pi/3; sin(theta) = 1/2 gives theta = pi/6, 5pi/6.

Step 6: 12. cosec(theta) = -2 gives theta = 7pi/6, 11pi/6; cos(theta) = 1/2 gives theta = pi/3, 5pi/3.

Answer: 7. theta = 5pi/6, 11pi/6 in [0, 2pi); 8. theta = pi/6, 5pi/6, 3pi/2; 9. theta = pi/2, 3pi/2; 10. theta = pi/6, 5pi/6; 11. theta = pi/6, pi/3, 5pi/6, 5pi/3; 12. theta = pi/3, 5pi/3, 7pi/6, 11pi/6

Worked Example: 13-22. Find the solution sets of the following equation. 13. tan(x) = 2sin(x); 14. 4sin^2(theta/2) - 3 = 0; 15. cos(2theta) = cos(theta); 16. sin(4x) - sin(2x) = cos(3x); 17. sin(x) + cos(3x) = cos(5x); 18. cos(x) + cos(3x) + cos(5x) = 0; 19. sin(theta) + sin(3theta) + sin(5theta) + sin(7theta) = 0; 20. cos(theta) + cos(3theta) + cos(5theta) + cos(7theta) = 0; 21. cosec(x) = √(3) + cot(x); 22. 2cos(theta) + sin^2(theta) - 1 = 0. (Flag: Q21 has an extraneous root — see steps. Q22 duplicates Q9 exactly.)

Formula used: Reduce to one ratio with sin^2 + cos^2 = 1 or sec^2 = 1 + tan^2; factorise; solve each factor by the general-solution formulas; reject roots outside the domain.

Step 1: 13. sin(x)(1 - 2cos(x)) = 0 with cos(x) not 0: x = n pi or x = +/-pi/3 + 2n pi.

Step 2: 14. sin(theta/2) = +/-√(3)/2, so theta = +/-2pi/3 + 2n pi.

Step 3: 15. 2theta = +/-theta + 2n pi, giving theta = 2n pi/3 (which contains both families).

Step 4: 16. 2cos(3x)sin(x) = cos(3x), so cos(3x)(2sin(x) - 1) = 0: x = pi/6 + n pi/3 or x = pi/6 + 2n pi, 5pi/6 + 2n pi.

Step 5: 17. sin(x) = cos(5x) - cos(3x) = -2sin(4x)sin(x), so sin(x)(1 + 2sin(4x)) = 0: x = n pi or x = 7pi/24 + n pi/2, 11pi/24 + n pi/2.

Step 6: 18. cos(3x)(2cos(2x) + 1) = 0: x = pi/6 + n pi/3 or x = pi/3 + n pi, 2pi/3 + n pi.

Step 7: 19. 4sin(4theta)cos(2theta)cos(theta) = 0. The cos factors give families contained in theta = n pi/4, so theta = n pi/4.

Step 8: 20. 4cos(4theta)cos(2theta)cos(theta) = 0: theta = pi/8 + n pi/4, pi/4 + n pi/2, pi/2 + n pi.

Step 9: 21. Multiplying by sin(x): 1 = √(3)sin(x) + cos(x), i.e. sin(x + pi/6) = 1/2, giving x = 2n pi or x = 2pi/3 + 2n pi. But x = 2n pi makes sin(x) = 0, where the original equation is undefined, so it is extraneous: x = 2pi/3 + 2n pi only.

Step 10: 22. As Q9: cos(theta)(2 - cos(theta)) = 0, so theta = pi/2 + n pi.

Answer: 13. x = n pi, +/-pi/3 + 2n pi; 14. theta = +/-2pi/3 + 2n pi; 15. theta = 2n pi/3; 16. x = pi/6 + n pi/3, 5pi/6 + 2n pi; 17. x = n pi, 7pi/24 + n pi/2, 11pi/24 + n pi/2; 18. x = pi/6 + n pi/3, pi/3 + n pi, 2pi/3 + n pi; 19. theta = n pi/4; 20. theta = pi/8 + n pi/4, pi/4 + n pi/2, pi/2 + n pi; 21. x = 2pi/3 + 2n pi only (see flag); 22. theta = pi/2 + n pi (duplicates Q9)

mcqs.q: The equation cosec(2theta) = 1/2 has:
mcqs.why: cosec(2theta)=1/2 means sin(2theta)=1/(1/2)=2. But |sin|<=1 always, so sin(2theta)=2 is impossible and there is NO solution.

mcqs.q: The general solution of cos(theta) = -1/2 is:
mcqs.why: Reference angle pi/3 since cos(pi/3)=1/2. Cosine negative in quadrants II and III: pi-pi/3=2pi/3 and pi+pi/3=4pi/3, each +2n pi.

mcqs.q: Solving cosec(3theta/2) = -2 gives theta equal to:
mcqs.why: cosec=-2 means sin(3theta/2)=-1/2, so 3theta/2=7pi/6+2n pi or 11pi/6+2n pi. Multiply by 2/3: theta=7pi/9+4n pi/3 or 11pi/9+4n pi/3.

mcqs.q: The general solution of sec^2(theta) = 4/3 is:
mcqs.why: sec^2=4/3 gives cos^2=3/4, so cos theta=+/-sqrt(3)/2. Both signs combine into theta=+/-pi/6+n pi, as worked in the notes.

mcqs.q: The general solution of 4 sin^2(theta) - 1 = 0 is:
mcqs.why: 4sin^2 theta=1 gives sin^2 theta=1/4, so sin theta=+/-1/2. The two signs combine into theta=+/-pi/6+n pi.

mcqs.q: The general solution of sec^2(theta) - 4 = 0 is:
mcqs.why: sec^2 theta=4 gives cos^2 theta=1/4, so cos theta=+/-1/2. Both signs combine into theta=+/-pi/3+n pi, as worked in the notes.

mcqs.q: In [0, 2pi), 3 tan^2(theta) + 2 sqrt(3) tan(theta) + 1 = 0 gives:
mcqs.why: The left side is (sqrt(3)tan theta+1)^2=0, so tan theta=-1/sqrt(3). In [0,2pi) this holds at pi-pi/6=5pi/6 and 2pi-pi/6=11pi/6.

mcqs.q: cot^2(theta) - cosec(theta) - 1 = 0 leads to cosec(theta) equal to:
mcqs.why: Use cot^2=cosec^2-1: cosec^2-cosec-2=0, factor (cosec-2)(cosec+1)=0, so cosec theta=2 or cosec theta=-1.

mcqs.q: 2 cos(theta) + sin^2(theta) - 1 = 0 reduces to:
mcqs.why: sin^2=1-cos^2 gives 2cos-cos^2=cos(2-cos)=0. cos=2 is impossible, so cos theta=0, giving theta=pi/2, 3pi/2 in [0,2pi).

mcqs.q: The solution set of tan(x) = 2 sin(x) is:
options: x = n pi or x = +/-pi/3 + 2n pi
mcqs.why: sin/cos=2sin gives sin(x)(1-2cos x)=0 with cos x not 0. sin x=0 gives x=n pi; cos x=1/2 gives x=+/-pi/3+2n pi.

lessons.title: Exercise 12.3 (p.358) - Applied Problems
lessons.notes_html:
Eight applied problems — lifts, ramps and angles — where the trigonometric equation must first be built from the situation, then solved for the angle in the stated range.

In this exercise: 1. Applied problems. 1. A hydraulic lift raises a platform 2m off the ground with the arm extending 5m. Find the angle between the arm and the ground. 2. In a mechanical linkage, a bar 10cm long.

Worked Example: 1-8. Applied problems. 1. A hydraulic lift raises a platform 2m off the ground with the arm extending 5m. Find the angle between the arm and the ground. 2. In a mechanical linkage, a bar 10cm long connects to a vertical support, forming a triangle with a horizontal base of 8cm. Find the angle of inclination. 3. A wheel chair ramp is 9m long and rises to a height of 1.5m. What is the angle of elevation. 4. From a point 30m from the base, an engineer measures an angle of elevation of 60 degrees. Find the height. 5. A boat is 100m from a light house. The angle of elevation to the top is 33 degrees. Find the height. 6. From a height of 200m, the angle of depression to a village is 12 degrees. Find the horizontal distance. 7. A drone at 120m observes a target on the ground at a 35 degrees angle. Find the distance to the target. 8. A model bridge ramp is 12cm long and rises 5cm. Find the angle it makes. (Flag for Q7: 'distance to the target' is ambiguous — both the slant distance and the horizontal distance are given.)

Formula used: Model first (sin or tan of the angle = opposite / hypotenuse or opposite / adjacent), then solve and keep only the angle that fits the situation.

Step 1: 1. sin(angle) = 2/5 = 0.4, so the angle is Sin^(-1)(0.4), about 23.6 degrees.

Step 2: 2. cos(angle) = 8/10 = 0.8, so the angle is Cos^(-1)(0.8), about 36.9 degrees.

Step 3: 3. sin(angle) = 1.5/9 = 1/6, so the angle is about 9.6 degrees.

Step 4: 4. Height = 30 x tan(60) = 30√(3), about 51.96 m.

Step 5: 5. Height = 100 x tan(33), about 64.94 m.

Step 6: 6. Horizontal distance = 200/tan(12), about 940.9 m.

Step 7: 7. Slant distance = 120/sin(35), about 209.2 m; horizontal distance = 120/tan(35), about 171.4 m.

Step 8: 8. sin(angle) = 5/12, so the angle is about 24.6 degrees.

Answer: 1. about 23.6 degrees; 2. about 36.9 degrees; 3. about 9.6 degrees; 4. about 51.96 m; 5. about 64.94 m; 6. about 940.9 m; 7. slant about 209.2 m, horizontal about 171.4 m (see flag); 8. about 24.6 degrees

mcqs.q: A hydraulic lift raises a platform 2 m with an arm of 5 m. The angle between arm and ground is about:
mcqs.why: Model: sin(angle)=opposite/hypotenuse=2/5=0.4. Angle=Sin^(-1)(0.4). In degrees arcsin(0.4) is about 23.58, i.e. about 23.6 degrees.

mcqs.q: A 10 cm bar with horizontal base 8 cm: the angle of inclination is about:
mcqs.why: Model: cos(angle)=adjacent/hypotenuse=8/10=0.8. Angle=Cos^(-1)(0.8). In degrees arccos(0.8) is about 36.87, i.e. about 36.9 degrees.

mcqs.q: A wheelchair ramp is 9 m long and rises 1.5 m. Its angle of elevation is about:
mcqs.why: Model: sin(angle)=rise/length=1.5/9=1/6 about 0.1667. Angle=Sin^(-1)(1/6), and arcsin(0.1667) in degrees is about 9.59, i.e. about 9.6 degrees.

mcqs.q: From 30 m away, angle of elevation 60 degrees: the height is about:
mcqs.why: Model: tan(60)=height/30, so height=30*tan(60)=30*sqrt(3). Numerically 30*1.732=51.96, so the height is about 51.96 m.

mcqs.q: A boat 100 m from a lighthouse, angle of elevation 33 degrees: the height is about:
mcqs.why: Model: tan(33)=height/100, so height=100*tan(33 degrees). tan(33) is about 0.6494, giving 100*0.6494=64.94 m.

mcqs.q: From 200 m height, angle of depression 12 degrees: the horizontal distance is about:
mcqs.why: Model: tan(12)=200/distance, so distance=200/tan(12 degrees). tan(12) is about 0.2126, giving 200/0.2126 about 940.9 m.

mcqs.q: A drone at 120 m, angle 35 degrees to a target: the slant distance to the target is about:
mcqs.why: Slant distance is the hypotenuse: sin(35)=120/slant, so slant=120/sin(35 degrees). sin(35) is about 0.5736, giving 120/0.5736 about 209.2 m.

mcqs.q: For the same drone (120 m, 35 degrees), the horizontal distance to the target is about:
mcqs.why: Horizontal distance uses tangent: tan(35)=120/horizontal, so horizontal=120/tan(35 degrees). tan(35) is about 0.7002, giving 120/0.7002 about 171.4 m.

mcqs.q: A model bridge ramp is 12 cm long and rises 5 cm. The angle it makes is about:
mcqs.why: Model: sin(angle)=rise/length=5/12 about 0.4167. Angle=Sin^(-1)(5/12), and arcsin(0.4167) in degrees is about 24.62, i.e. about 24.6 degrees.

mcqs.q: For the hydraulic lift (rise 2 m, arm 5 m), the correct model equation is:
mcqs.why: The rise is opposite the angle and the 5 m arm is the hypotenuse, so sin(angle)=opposite/hypotenuse=2/5. The form 5/2 exceeds 1 and cannot be a sine.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 12 (pp.358-359)
lessons.notes_html:
Review of Unit 12: general solutions, graphical solutions on a short interval, and domain traps.

In this exercise: 1. Choose the correct options. 2. Using graph, find the solution of the following equations for -pi/2 <= theta <= pi/2. 3. Find the solution of the following trigonometric equations. tan^2(theta) - sec(theta) - 1 = 0. 4. 4sin^2(theta) - 8cos(theta) + 1 = 0. 5. sec(3theta) = sec(theta). 6. A display ramp is 8cm long with a 2.5cm rise. What is the angle of elevation.

Worked Example: 1(i). If alpha = tan^(-1)(1) and beta = tan^(-1)(1/√(3)) where alpha and beta lie in first quadrant then alpha + beta is;

a) pi/6   b) pi/4   c) pi/3   d) 5pi/12

Answer: d) 5pi/12

Worked Example: 1(ii). If cos(theta) = -√(3)/2 and 0 < theta < pi then theta is;

a) pi/6   b) pi/3   c) 2pi/3   d) 5pi/6

Answer: d) 5pi/6

Worked Example: 1(iii). The general solution of cos^2(theta) = 3/4 is;

a) pi/6 + 2n pi, 5pi/6 + 2n pi, n in Z   b) pi/3 + 2n pi, 5pi/3 + 2n pi, n in Z   c) pi/4 + 2n pi, 3pi/4 + 2n pi, n in Z   d) pi/2 + 2n pi, pi + 2n pi, n in Z

Answer: a) pi/6 + 2n pi, 5pi/6 + 2n pi, n in Z

Note: No printed option is fully correct: cos(theta) = +/-√(3)/2 gives four families theta = pi/6, 5pi/6, 7pi/6, 11pi/6, each + 2n pi. Option (a) is the intended one.

Worked Example: 1(iv). The general solution of sin^2(theta) - 3sin(theta) + 2 = 0 is;

a) pi + 2n pi, n in Z   b) pi/2 + 2n pi, n in Z   c) pi/6 + 2n pi, n in Z   d) pi/3 + 2n pi, n in Z

Answer: b) pi/2 + 2n pi, n in Z

Worked Example: 1(v). If cos(theta) = -1/2, then theta is;

a) 30 degrees   b) 60 degrees   c) 90 degrees   d) 120 degrees

Answer: d) 120 degrees

Worked Example: 2. Using graph, find the solution of the following equations for -pi/2 <= theta <= pi/2. (i) 2cos(theta) - theta = 0; (ii) sin(theta) = 1 + theta. (Flag: (ii) has NO solution in this interval — see steps.)

Formula used: See the formulas in the Unit 12 Overview and Lessons 1 to 3 of this unit.

Step 1: (i) 2cos(theta) = theta is the same equation as Ex 12.1 Q13: cos(theta) = theta/2, crossing once at theta about 1.03.

Step 2: (ii) sin(theta) - 1 - theta has derivative cos(theta) - 1 <= 0, so it is decreasing, and it is already negative at theta = -pi/2 (about -0.43) and at theta = 0 (-1). Hence it never reaches 0: NO solution in this interval.

Answer: (i) theta about 1.03; (ii) NO solution

Worked Example: 3. Find the solution of the following trigonometric equations. tan^2(theta) - sec(theta) - 1 = 0.

Formula used: See the formulas in the Unit 12 Overview and Lessons 1 to 3 of this unit.

Step 1: Using tan^2 = sec^2 - 1: sec^2(theta) - sec(theta) - 2 = 0, so (sec(theta) - 2)(sec(theta) + 1) = 0.

Step 2: sec(theta) = 2 gives theta = +/-pi/3 + 2n pi; sec(theta) = -1 gives theta = pi + 2n pi.

Answer: theta = +/-pi/3 + 2n pi, pi + 2n pi

Worked Example: 5. sec(3theta) = sec(theta). (Flag: the raw families theta = n pi and theta = n pi/2 must be cut by the domain — sec is undefined where cos = 0, which removes the odd multiples of pi/2, leaving theta = n pi.)

Formula used: See the formulas in the Unit 12 Overview and Lessons 1 to 3 of this unit.

Step 1: sec(3theta) = sec(theta) gives 3theta = +/-theta + 2n pi, i.e. theta = n pi or theta = n pi/2.

Step 2: But sec(theta) is undefined at theta = pi/2 + n pi, so the odd multiples of pi/2 are excluded, leaving theta = n pi.

Answer: theta = n pi (see flag)

Worked Example: 6. A display ramp is 8cm long with a 2.5cm rise. What is the angle of elevation?

Formula used: See the formulas in the Unit 12 Overview and Lessons 1 to 3 of this unit.

Step 1: sin(angle) = 2.5/8 = 0.3125, so the angle is about 18.2 degrees.

Answer: about 18.2 degrees

mcqs.q: If alpha = Tan^(-1)(1) and beta = Tan^(-1)(1/sqrt(3)) in the first quadrant, alpha + beta is:
mcqs.why: alpha=Tan^(-1)(1)=pi/4 and beta=Tan^(-1)(1/sqrt(3))=pi/6. Sum=pi/4+pi/6=(3pi+2pi)/12=5pi/12.

mcqs.q: If cos(theta) = -sqrt(3)/2 and 0 < theta < pi, then theta is:
mcqs.why: Reference angle pi/6 since cos(pi/6)=sqrt(3)/2. Cosine negative in quadrant II within (0,pi): theta=pi-pi/6=5pi/6. Check cos(5pi/6)=-sqrt(3)/2.

mcqs.q: The FULL general solution of cos^2(theta) = 3/4 is:
mcqs.why: cos^2=3/4 gives cos theta=+/-sqrt(3)/2. Positive gives pi/6, 11pi/6; negative gives 5pi/6, 7pi/6, each +2n pi. The book's option (a) lists only two families and is incomplete.

mcqs.q: The general solution of sin^2(theta) - 3 sin(theta) + 2 = 0 is:
mcqs.why: Factor: (sin theta-1)(sin theta-2)=0, so sin theta=1 or 2. sin=2 is impossible; sin theta=1 gives theta=pi/2+2n pi.

mcqs.q: If cos(theta) = -1/2 (principal acute-obtuse value), theta in degrees is:
mcqs.why: cos(120 degrees)=cos(2pi/3)=-1/2. Reference angle is 60 degrees and cosine is negative in quadrant II: 180-60=120 degrees.

mcqs.q: Using a graph on -pi/2 <= theta <= pi/2, 2 cos(theta) - theta = 0 gives:
mcqs.why: 2cos theta=theta is cos theta=theta/2, the same as Ex 12.1 Q13. Check theta=1.03: cos(1.03) about 0.515 and 1.03/2=0.515, so theta is about 1.03.

mcqs.q: Using a graph on -pi/2 <= theta <= pi/2, sin(theta) = 1 + theta has:
mcqs.why: sin theta-1-theta has derivative cos theta-1<=0, so it decreases; at theta=-pi/2 it is already about -0.43 and at 0 it is -1, so it never reaches 0: NO solution.

mcqs.q: tan^2(theta) - sec(theta) - 1 = 0 gives sec(theta) equal to:
mcqs.why: Use tan^2=sec^2-1: sec^2-sec-2=0, factor (sec-2)(sec+1)=0, so sec theta=2 or sec theta=-1, giving theta=+/-pi/3+2n pi and pi+2n pi.

mcqs.q: After cutting by the domain, sec(3theta) = sec(theta) gives:
mcqs.why: Raw families: 3theta=+/-theta+2n pi gives theta=n pi or n pi/2. But sec is undefined at pi/2+n pi, so odd multiples of pi/2 are removed, leaving theta=n pi.

mcqs.q: A display ramp is 8 cm long with a 2.5 cm rise. Its angle of elevation is about:
mcqs.why: Model: sin(angle)=rise/length=2.5/8=0.3125. Angle=Sin^(-1)(0.3125), and arcsin(0.3125) in degrees is about 18.21, i.e. about 18.2 degrees.
